about.title: How Devanagari works
about.text:
Hindi is written in the Devanagari script, from left to right. There are no capital letters. Most letters hang from a horizontal line along the top, and the letters of one word share one continuous line, so the breaks in the line show you where words end.

Devanagari is not an alphabet of separate vowels and consonants like English. Each consonant letter stands for a whole syllable: the consonant plus a short 'a'. So क is not 'k' but 'ka'. To get any other vowel you attach a vowel sign to the consonant. Vowels have a full, independent letter only when they begin a syllable on their own, usually at the start of a word.

The great advantage for a learner is that Hindi spelling is very regular. Once you know the letters and three or four rules explained below, you can read any word aloud correctly, which you cannot do in English.

A sentence ends with a vertical bar called the danda (।) instead of a full stop. Question marks, commas and exclamation marks are the same as in English.

about.title: The inherent vowel and the vowel signs
about.text:
Every consonant carries the short vowel 'a' (the sound of the a in 'about') unless something changes it. To change it, a vowel sign (called a matra) is written on the consonant: after it, before it, above it or below it.

There are ten vowel signs to learn, one for each vowel other than 'a'. On the consonant क they look like this: का kaa, कि ki, की kee, कु ku, कू koo, के ke, कै kai, को ko, कौ kau, and कृ kri.

Two things surprise beginners. First, the sign for short i (ि) is written to the LEFT of its consonant but pronounced AFTER it: कि is 'ki', not 'ik'. Second, र takes the u-signs in the middle of the letter rather than underneath: रु is 'ru' and रू is 'roo'.

Vowel length matters and changes meaning. Short a, i, u are quick and relaxed; aa, ee, oo are held about twice as long.

about.title: When the built-in 'a' is silent
about.text:
Although every consonant letter contains an 'a', Hindi does not pronounce all of them. Dropping it follows two dependable rules.

Rule 1: the 'a' of the last consonant of a word is silent. कमल is 'kamal', not 'kamala'; घर is 'ghar'; नाम is 'naam'. A one-letter word keeps its vowel (न 'na').

Rule 2: inside a word, the 'a' is usually dropped from a consonant that stands between two pronounced syllables, when the next consonant carries a vowel sign. लड़का is 'larkaa', not 'larakaa'; करना is 'karnaa'; आदमी is 'aadmee'. This is why the same root can sound different in different forms: समझ is 'samajh' but समझा is 'samjhaa'; निकल is 'nikal' but निकला is 'niklaa'.

The romanisation in this course always shows the word as it is actually spoken, so you can trust it. Where the 'a' is written but silent, it is simply left out of the romanisation.

about.title: Breathy and plain consonants
about.text:
English has one 'k', one 'p', one 't'. Hindi has two of each: a plain one and one with a strong puff of breath (aspirated). They are different letters and they change the meaning of a word.

Plain: क ka, च cha, ट ta, त ta, प pa and the voiced ग ga, ज ja, ड da, द da, ब ba. Breathy: ख kha, छ chha, ठ tha, थ tha, फ pha and the voiced घ gha, झ jha, ढ dha, ध dha, भ bha. In the romanisation the breathy ones always have an h.

The trap: English speakers automatically puff the k, p, t at the start of a word ('kit', 'pin', 'top'). To a Hindi ear that is ख, फ, ठ. For plain क, प, त hold your breath back, as in English 'skin', 'spin', 'stop'. Hold a hand in front of your mouth: for क you should feel almost nothing, for ख a clear puff.

Note that 'th' in this course is never the English 'th' of 'think': it is a t followed by breath. Likewise 'ph' is p plus breath (though many speakers say it as f), and 'chh' is a breathy ch.

about.title: Tongue on the teeth or curled back
about.text:
Hindi has two series of t and d sounds, and neither is quite the English one.

Dental: त, थ, द, ध, न. The tip of the tongue touches the back of the upper front teeth, as in Spanish or Italian. These sound soft.

Retroflex: ट, ठ, ड, ढ, ण. The tip of the tongue curls back and touches the roof of the mouth behind the gum ridge. These sound hard and hollow. English t and d sound retroflex to Hindi speakers, which is why English words are written with them: टिकट (ticket), डॉक्टर (doctor).

There are also two flapped sounds, ड़ and ढ़ (the letters ड and ढ with a dot below). The tongue curls back and flicks forward once, giving a sound between r and d. They never begin a word.

Important: to stay easy to read and to say, the romanisation in this course does NOT mark the difference. Both त and ट are written 't', both द and ड are 'd', and ड़ is written 'r' (ढ़ is 'rh'). The Devanagari always tells you which one is meant, so read the Hindi spelling, and learn each new word with the right tongue position.

about.title: Nasal sounds: the dot and the moon-dot
about.text:
Two signs written above the line make nasal sounds.

The chandrabindu (ँ, 'moon-dot') nasalises a vowel: the vowel is spoken through the nose and mouth together, as in French 'bon', and no separate n is pronounced. हाँ (yes), माँ (mother), कहाँ (where), हूँ (am).

The anusvara (ं, a single dot) properly stands for a nasal consonant before another consonant: n before t, d, k, g, ch, j, and m before p, b. So हिंदी is 'hindee' and लंबा is 'lambaa'. The same words may also be spelt with a half consonant: हिन्दी, लम्बा. Both spellings are correct; the dot is the commoner modern one.

When a vowel sign already sits above the line there is no room for the moon, so the plain dot is written even though the vowel is nasalised: मैं (I), में (in), हैं (are), नहीं (not), क्यों (why). You simply learn that these very common words end in a nasal vowel.

In the romanisation both signs appear as 'n' (or 'm' before p and b). At the end of a word, or before h, s, or a vowel, that n is not a real n: it only tells you to nasalise the vowel before it. So हाँ is 'haan', पाँच is 'paanch' and हैं is 'hain', distinct from है 'hai'.

about.title: Joined consonants
about.text:
When two consonants come together with no vowel between them, the first one loses its 'a' and the two are written as one joined letter, a conjunct.

Most conjuncts are easy to read: the first consonant loses its right-hand vertical stroke and leans against the second. स + त gives स्त as in नमस्ते (namaste); च + छ gives च्छ as in अच्छा (achchhaa); न + द gives न्द.

A few have special shapes that must be learnt as letters in their own right: क्ष (ksha), त्र (tra), ज्ञ (pronounced gya in Hindi) and श्र (shra).

The letter र behaves differently. When r comes BEFORE another consonant it is written as a hook above the following letter: गर्म (garm, hot), शर्ट (shart, shirt). When r comes AFTER a consonant it is a small slanting stroke at the foot of that consonant: प्र (pra), क्र (kra); under ट and ड it looks like a little hat: ट्र (tra).

The sign that removes the 'a' is called the halant or virama (्). You seldom see it printed on its own, but it is what you type between two consonants to join them.

A doubled consonant is really held longer: बच्चा is 'bach-chaa', पक्का is 'pak-kaa'.

about.title: Dotted letters and borrowed sounds
about.text:
A dot placed BELOW a letter (the nukta) makes a new sound.

Two dotted letters, ड़ and ढ़, are native Hindi flaps and are always written with the dot.

Five others spell sounds that came in with Persian, Arabic and English words: ज़ (z), फ़ (f), क़ (q), ख़ (kh as in Scottish 'loch') and ग़ (a gargled g). In everyday speech nearly everyone pronounces z and f, so this course always writes ज़ and फ़ with their dots: ज़रूर (zaroor), फ़ोन (fon). The other three are pronounced as plain क, ख, ग by most speakers and are very often printed without the dot, so in the lessons this course writes them without it: खबर, गलत, कीमत. You will meet both spellings in real life.

You will also see the dot left off ज़ and फ़ in careless print; a word such as बाज़ार may appear as बाजार. Pronounce the z anyway.

Finally, English words with the short o of 'hot' or 'coffee' are written with a small crescent over the long-a sign: ऑ. डॉक्टर (doctor), कॉफ़ी (coffee), ऑफ़िस (office). It is romanised here as 'o'.

about.title: Where the sound differs from the spelling
about.text:
Hindi spelling is regular, but a handful of habits are worth knowing from the first day.

1. Short 'a' next to ह. When a short a comes before ह, and often on both sides of it, it is pronounced like the e in 'get'. So बहन (written bahan) sounds like 'behen', पहले like 'pehle', कहना like 'kehnaa', रहना like 'rehnaa', शहर like 'sheher', and बहुत is often 'bohot'. This course writes these with 'a' (bahan, pahle) so that the romanisation stays regular; say them with the 'e' sound.

2. यह and वह. These two tiny words, 'this' and 'that/he/she', are written yah and vah but in conversation are almost always pronounced 'ye' and 'vo'. Their plurals ये (ye) and वे (ve) are spelt as they sound, though in speech वे is usually 'vo' as well. छह (six) is likewise said 'chhe'.

3. ऐ and औ are not the 'ai' of 'aisle' and the 'ow' of 'cow'. In standard Hindi ऐ is an open e, like the a in 'cat' or the e in 'bed' held long (है, मैं, पैसा), and औ is an open o, like the 'aw' in 'saw' (और, कौन, नौ).

4. ज्ञ is written j + ny but pronounced 'gy': ज्ञान is 'gyaan'.

5. ऋ is pronounced 'ri': ऋषि is 'rishi', कृपया is 'kripayaa'.

6. व lies between English v and w. Use a soft v with the lips barely touching the teeth.

7. Stress is light and even. Do not hammer one syllable as English does; give every syllable its length, long vowels long and short vowels short.

about.title: The romanisation used in this course
about.text:
Every Hindi word in this course is also given in Latin letters, always in lower case. The scheme is simple and is used the same way everywhere.

Vowels: a (अ, as in 'about'), aa (आ, 'father'), i (इ, 'sit'), ee (ई, 'see'), u (उ, 'put'), oo (ऊ, 'food'), e (ए, like 'day' without the glide), ai (ऐ, open e as in 'bed'), o (ओ, like 'go' without the glide), au (औ, 'saw'), ri (ऋ). The o of English loanwords (ऑ) is also written o.

Consonants: an h after a consonant means a puff of breath: kh, gh, chh, jh, th, dh, ph, bh. 'ch' is always as in 'church', 'g' always as in 'go', 'sh' covers both श and ष, 'v' is व, 'z' is ज़, 'f' is फ़, 'gy' is ज्ञ, 'ksh' is क्ष.

Not marked: dental and retroflex t, th, d, dh, n look the same in romanisation; the flaps ड़ and ढ़ are written r and rh. Check the Devanagari.

Nasal vowels: written with n (haan, main, naheen, kyon). A final n after a long vowel in such words is not a full n.

Between vowels: when two vowels meet, they are written side by side (bhaaee, koee, gaee, aaiye). The polite ending -इए is written 'iye'.

Silent letters are not written (see the section on the silent 'a'), and doubled consonants are written double (achchhaa, bachche, pakkaa).

units.title: Greetings & basics
units.description: Say hello and goodbye, ask how someone is, thank people and apologise.

guide.title: One greeting for every hour
guide.text:
नमस्ते (namaste) works at any time of day, to anyone, for both hello and goodbye. It is usually said with the palms pressed together in front of the chest and a slight nod. नमस्कार (namaskaar) means the same and sounds a little more formal; you hear it in speeches, on the news and when greeting a group.

Hindi has no everyday equivalent of 'good morning' or 'good afternoon'. Phrases such as शुभ रात्रि (shubh raatri, good night) exist, but they are bookish; in ordinary life people say नमस्ते again, or use the English phrase. When you leave, नमस्ते or फिर मिलेंगे (phir milenge, 'we will meet again') is enough.

You will also hear greetings tied to a community, such as सलाम (salaam) or आदाब (aadaab) among Muslims and सत श्री अकाल (sat shree akaal) among Sikhs. नमस्ते is understood and welcome everywhere.

guide.title: Asking how someone is
guide.text:
The question is आप कैसे हैं? (aap kaise hain?), word for word 'you how are?'. Notice two things that hold for all of Hindi: the verb comes last, and the question word sits just before it.

कैसे is said to a man. To a woman the word takes the feminine ending: आप कैसी हैं? (aap kaisee hain?). It is the person you are talking to who decides the ending, not your own gender.

The usual answers are मैं ठीक हूँ (main theek hoon, 'I am fine'), बढ़िया (barhiyaa, 'great'), or सब ठीक है (sab theek hai, 'all is well'). Then return the question with और आप? (aur aap?, 'and you?').

guide.title: Thank you and sorry
guide.text:
धन्यवाद (dhanyavaad) is the formal, Sanskrit-derived 'thank you'; शुक्रिया (shukriyaa), from Persian, is just as common in conversation, and so is the English 'thank you'. All three are fine.

A cultural point: between family members and close friends thanks are said far less often than in English, because saying them can create distance. With strangers, shopkeepers and hosts, thank freely.

माफ़ कीजिए (maaf keejiye) literally asks 'please forgive'. It covers both 'sorry' and 'excuse me'. The standard reply to either thanks or an apology is कोई बात नहीं (koee baat naheen), 'it's nothing'.

guide.title: The little word jee
guide.text:
जी (jee) is a marker of respect with no exact English equivalent. Put before हाँ (yes) or नहीं (no) it makes the answer polite: जी हाँ, जी नहीं. Put after a name or a title it works like 'Mr', 'Mrs' or 'sir': राज जी, डॉक्टर जी, पिताजी (father).

On its own, जी can mean 'yes', or with a rising tone 'pardon?'. You cannot overuse it with people older than you or people you have just met.

units.title: Introductions
units.description: Say who you are, where you are from and what you do, and ask the same of someone else.

guide.title: My name is ...
guide.text:
मेरा नाम ... है (meraa naam ... hai) is 'my name ... is'. The name goes in the middle and the verb है (is) comes last. To ask, put क्या (kyaa, what) where the name would go: आपका नाम क्या है? 'your name what is?'.

मेरा means 'my' and आपका means 'your' (polite). You will learn in a later unit that these words change their ending to match the thing owned; नाम (name) is masculine, so they end in -aa here.

Hindi has no word for 'a' or 'the'. मैं विद्यार्थी हूँ is simply 'I student am'.

guide.title: Words like 'from' and 'in' come after the noun
guide.text:
English has prepositions: 'from America', 'in Delhi'. Hindi has postpositions: the little word follows the noun. अमेरिका से (amerikaa se) is 'America from'; दिल्ली में (dillee mein) is 'Delhi in'.

So 'I am from America' is built as मैं अमेरिका से हूँ, 'I America from am'. Swap in your own country: इंग्लैंड (inglaind, England), ऑस्ट्रेलिया (ostreliyaa, Australia), कनाडा (kanaadaa, Canada).

guide.title: Your verbs show whether you are a man or a woman
guide.text:
Many Hindi verb forms end in -aa for a masculine subject and -ee for a feminine one. So a man and a woman say 'I live', 'I am learning' or 'I have come' slightly differently.

A man says मैं रहता हूँ (main rahtaa hoon), a woman says मैं रहती हूँ (main rahtee hoon). A man says आया हूँ (aayaa hoon, 'have come'), a woman आई हूँ (aaee hoon).

The same applies when you speak to someone: आप क्या काम करते हैं? to a man, आप क्या काम करती हैं? to a woman. Throughout this course the main phrase gives the masculine form and the note gives the feminine one.

guide.title: Introducing someone with respect
guide.text:
To introduce a person, Hindi uses the plural out of respect, even for one person: ये मेरे दोस्त हैं, word for word 'these my friends are', means 'this is my friend'. The singular यह मेरा दोस्त है is used for a child, or between young friends.

After the introduction say आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई (aapse milkar khushee huee), 'having met you, happiness happened'.

phrases.note: Replace 'raaj' with your own name.
'se' means 'from' and comes after the place.
To a woman: आप क्या काम करती हैं? (... kartee hain?)
The English word 'student' (स्टूडेंट) is also very common in speech.
Most modern job titles are simply the English word: डॉक्टर (doktar), टीचर (teechar), मैनेजर (mainejar).

phrases.english: I am here on a visit.
phrases.note: A woman says: मैं यहाँ घूमने आई हूँ (... aaee hoon).
To a woman: आप कहाँ रहती हैं? (... rahtee hain?)
A woman says: मैं दिल्ली में रहती हूँ (... rahtee hoon).
A woman says: मैं हिंदी सीख रही हूँ (... seekh rahee hoon).
Languages and skills 'come to' you in Hindi. The sentence is the same for men and women, because the verb agrees with हिंदी.
The plural form is used for one person to show respect. The same sentence can also mean 'These are my friends'.

units.title: Yes, no and polite words
units.description: Agree, refuse, get someone's attention and sound polite while doing it.

guide.title: Yes and no
guide.text:
हाँ (haan) is yes and नहीं (naheen) is no. Both end in a nasal vowel: let the sound come through the nose and do not pronounce a clear n. On their own they are casual, fine with friends. With anyone older or unfamiliar add जी: जी हाँ, जी नहीं.

In practice people often answer a question by repeating its verb instead of saying yes: 'Are you coming?' 'Coming.' And a bare जी (jee) is a very common respectful 'yes'.

A famous gesture: the Indian head wobble, tilting the head from side to side, means 'yes', 'okay' or 'I am listening'. It is not a 'no'.

guide.title: How Hindi says 'please'
guide.text:
Hindi does have a word for please, कृपया (kripayaa), but it belongs to notices and announcements ('Please stand clear of the doors'). In conversation it sounds stiff.

Everyday politeness is built into the verb. The ending -इए (-iye) turns a verb into a polite request all by itself: आइए (aaiye, 'please come'), बैठिए (baithiye, 'please sit'), सुनिए (suniye, 'please listen'). When English says 'please', Hindi usually just uses this ending together with आप, the polite 'you'.

To soften a request further add ज़रा (zaraa, 'just a little') at the front: ज़रा सुनिए, 'could you just listen a moment'.

examples.english: Excuse me, could you listen a moment

guide.title: The many meanings of achchhaa
guide.text:
अच्छा (achchhaa) literally means 'good', but it is also the commonest reaction word in Hindi and its meaning depends on the tone.

Said flatly, it is 'okay, fine'. With a rising tone, अच्छा? is 'really? is that so?'. Drawn out, it is 'oh, I see'. At the start of a sentence it is 'well then' or 'right', often used to wind up a conversation: अच्छा, फिर मिलेंगे, 'right, see you then'.

Other handy reaction words are ज़रूर (zaroor, 'certainly'), शायद (shaayad, 'maybe') and बिलकुल (bilkul, 'absolutely'; also spelt बिल्कुल).

guide.title: Getting someone's attention
guide.text:
To stop a stranger, a waiter or a shopkeeper, say सुनिए (suniye), literally 'please listen'. It does the job of 'excuse me'.

People are also addressed with family words rather than 'sir' or 'madam'. A man of roughly your own age is भैया (bhaiyaa) or भाई साहब (bhaaee saahab), 'brother'; a woman is दीदी (deedee, 'elder sister') or बहन जी (bahan jee); older people are अंकल and आंटी (uncle, aunty). This is friendly and normal, not over-familiar.

When someone turns to help you they may say जी, बताइए (jee, bataaiye): 'yes, tell me'.

phrases.note: The vowel is nasal; do not pronounce a clear n at the end.
Also the word for 'not'.
Also added after names and titles to show respect.
Mostly written or announced. In speech the polite verb ending -iye does the work of 'please'.
The meaning depends on the tone of voice.
Also spelt बिल्कुल.
Literally 'please listen'.
Said at a doorway or when offering food. 'pahle' is pronounced 'pehle'.
The usual reply to both 'sorry' and 'thank you'.

units.title: Numbers 1-10
units.description: Count from zero to ten and say how many of something you want.

guide.title: Counting to ten
guide.text:
The numbers one to ten are एक, दो, तीन, चार, पाँच, छह, सात, आठ, नौ, दस. They never change: there is no masculine or feminine form, and no special form before a postposition.

Pronunciation points. तीन (teen), सात (saat) and दस (das) have dental t and d, with the tongue on the teeth; आठ (aath) ends in a retroflex, breathy t. पाँच (paanch) has a nasal vowel. छह is written chhah but is nearly always said 'chhe'. नौ (nau) has the open o of 'saw'.

Hindi has its own digits (१ २ ३ ...), shown in the notes and in the Letters section. On price tags, phones, clocks and banknotes you will mostly see the international digits 1, 2, 3.

guide.title: Number + noun
guide.text:
The number goes before the noun, as in English: दो चाय (do chaay, 'two teas'), तीन लोग (teen log, 'three people').

एक (ek) also does duty for 'a/an' when you want to stress that it is one thing: एक चाय दीजिए, 'one tea, please' or 'a tea, please'.

Nouns do have plural forms, which you will meet gradually. The two commonest patterns: masculine nouns ending in -aa change it to -e (लड़का larkaa, 'boy' becomes दो लड़के do larke, 'two boys'), and feminine nouns ending in a consonant add -en (किताब kitaab, 'book' becomes दो किताबें do kitaaben). Many masculine nouns do not change at all: एक घर, दो घर ('one house, two houses').

guide.title: How many?
guide.text:
'How many' is कितने (kitne) for masculine things and people in general, and कितनी (kitnee) for feminine things. Asked on its own, कितने? is enough.

To answer, the number alone will do, or number plus noun. When ordering or buying, end with दीजिए (deejiye, 'please give'): दो चाय दीजिए, 'two teas, please'.

phrases.note: Numeral: ०. When reading out phone numbers people usually say 'zero' in English.
Numeral: १
Numeral: २
Numeral: ३
Numeral: ४
Numeral: ५. The vowel is nasalised.
Numeral: ६. Usually pronounced 'chhe'.
Numeral: ७
Numeral: ८
Numeral: ९
Numeral: १०
For feminine things: कितनी? (kitnee?)
A useful answer when a restaurant asks how many you are.

units.title: Word order and 'to be'
units.description: Build simple sentences with am, is and are, and put the words in the Hindi order.

guide.title: The verb comes last
guide.text:
English order is subject, verb, object: 'I drink tea'. Hindi order is subject, object, verb: 'I tea drink'. Whatever else is in the sentence, the verb goes to the end.

So 'This is a book' becomes यह किताब है, 'this book is'. 'I am at home' becomes मैं घर पर हूँ, 'I home at am'.

Descriptions go before the verb too: चाय गर्म है, 'tea hot is'. And as you saw in the first lessons, words like 'in', 'at' and 'from' follow their noun. A good way to think of a Hindi sentence is as an English sentence read largely backwards from the end.

guide.title: Am, is, are
guide.text:
The verb 'to be' is होना (honaa). Its present forms are few, and you will use them in almost every sentence, because they are also the helping verb of most tenses.

मैं हूँ (main hoon): I am.
तुम हो (tum ho): you are, to a friend.
आप हैं (aap hain): you are, polite.
यह है, वह है (yah hai, vah hai): this is, that is; he, she, it is.
हम हैं (ham hain): we are.
ये हैं, वे हैं (ye hain, ve hain): these are, those are, they are.

The only difference between है (is) and हैं (are) is the nasal dot. Listen for it and say it: hai against hain. हैं is used with every plural subject and with आप, even when आप is one person.

examples.english: He is a doctor. / She is a doctor.

guide.title: No 'a', no 'the', no 'it'
guide.text:
Hindi has no articles. किताब can be 'a book' or 'the book'; the situation tells you which. If you need to stress 'one, a certain', use एक (ek): एक किताब.

There is also no separate word for 'he', 'she' and 'it'. वह (vah, usually pronounced 'vo') covers all three, plus 'that'; यह (yah, pronounced 'ye') is 'this' and also 'he, she, it' for someone or something close by. The gender shows up elsewhere in the sentence, in adjectives and verbs.

And where English needs a dummy 'it' or 'there' ('it is cold', 'there is a problem'), Hindi just leaves it out.

guide.title: Was and were
guide.text:
The past of 'to be' changes for gender and number, not for person. था (thaa) is for one masculine subject, थी (thee) for one feminine subject, थे (the) for masculine plural and for आप said to a man, and थीं (theen) for feminine plural and for आप said to a woman.

So a man says मैं यहाँ था ('I was here') and a woman says मैं यहाँ थी. To a man you say आप कहाँ थे? and to a woman आप कहाँ थीं?

phrases.note: The same sentence means 'She is a doctor'. To speak respectfully of an adult, use the plural: वे डॉक्टर हैं (ve doktar hain).
To a woman: आप बहुत अच्छी हैं (aap bahut achchhee hain).
गर्म is also written and said गरम (garam).
A woman says: मैं थकी हुई हूँ (main thakee huee hoon).
Polite: आप कहाँ हैं? (aap kahaan hain?)
'She was here' is वह यहाँ थी (vah yahaan thee).

units.title: Pronouns and respect
units.description: Choose the right word for 'you', and talk about he, she and they with the right level of respect.

guide.title: Three words for 'you'
guide.text:
Hindi has three levels of 'you', and each has its own verb form.

आप (aap) is polite. Use it with strangers, anyone older, colleagues, shopkeepers, in-laws, and whenever you are unsure. It takes the plural verb: आप कैसे हैं? This course uses आप by default, and you can never go wrong with it.

तुम (tum) is familiar. Friends of the same age use it with each other; adults use it to children and to younger relatives. It has its own verb form ending in -o: तुम कैसे हो?

तू (too) is intimate. It is used with small children, between very close friends, to God, and also in anger or contempt. It takes the singular verb: तू कैसा है? As a learner, understand it but do not use it.

Moving from आप to तुम is a sign of growing friendship; let the Hindi speaker make the move first.

guide.title: He, she, it, they
guide.text:
There is one set of words for 'he', 'she' and 'it', chosen by distance rather than gender.

यह (yah, said 'ye'): this; he, she or it, close by.
वह (vah, said 'vo'): that; he, she or it, further away or not present. This is the usual word for 'he' and 'she'.
ये (ye): these; they, close by.
वे (ve, usually said 'vo'): those; they.

Gender appears in the words around the pronoun. वह मेरा दोस्त है is 'he is my friend'; वह मेरी दोस्त है is 'she is my friend': only 'my' changes.

Respect matters here too. To speak respectfully about one person (a parent, a teacher, an older stranger, your friend's spouse) use the plural ये or वे with a plural verb: वे मेरे शिक्षक हैं, 'he is my teacher', literally 'they are my teachers'. Using the singular वह for an elder sounds disrespectful.

guide.title: The whole set with 'to be'
guide.text:
Here are all the pronouns with the present of 'to be'. Learn them as pairs, because the same endings return in every tense.

मैं हूँ: I am. तू है: you are (intimate). तुम हो: you are (familiar). आप हैं: you are (polite). यह है, वह है: he, she, it is. हम हैं: we are. ये हैं, वे हैं: they are.

In several regions people say हम (ham, 'we') when they mean 'I'. You do not need to copy this, but do not be surprised by it.

examples.english: You are very nice. (to a male friend)

guide.title: Making it clear you mean several people
guide.text:
Because आप, वे and even हम can refer to one person, Hindi adds लोग (log, 'people') when it really means more than one: आप लोग ('you all'), हम लोग ('we, all of us'), वे लोग ('those people, they').

The verb is plural in any case; लोग only removes the doubt.

phrases.note: To a female friend: तुम कैसी हो? (tum kaisee ho?)
Only for small children and the closest friends. Learn to recognise it; use तुम or आप yourself.
Only मेरी (my, feminine) shows that the friend is a woman. A woman's female friend is also called सहेली (sahelee).
Plural for respect. Of a woman teacher: वे मेरी शिक्षिका हैं (ve meree shikshikaa hain). In speech the English word 'teacher' (टीचर) is more usual.
भी (also) comes straight after the word it applies to.

phrases.english: You are very nice. (to a friend)
phrases.note: To a female friend: तुम बहुत अच्छी हो (tum bahut achchhee ho).

units.title: My, your, his
units.description: Say whose something is, with my, your, his, her, our, their and the Hindi 's.

guide.title: My, your, our
guide.text:
The possessive words are: मेरा (meraa, my), हमारा (hamaaraa, our), तुम्हारा (tumhaaraa, your, familiar), आपका (aapkaa, your, polite), and तेरा (teraa, your, intimate).

The key rule: these words behave like adjectives and agree with the thing owned, NOT with the owner. Before a masculine singular noun they end in -aa, before a feminine noun in -ee, and before a masculine plural noun (or a respected person) in -e.

So both a man and a woman say मेरा घर (my house, masculine), मेरी किताब (my book, feminine) and मेरे बच्चे (my children, plural). Whether the speaker is male or female makes no difference.

Every Hindi noun is either masculine or feminine, and you have to learn the gender with the noun. A rough guide: nouns ending in -aa are mostly masculine (कमरा, लड़का), nouns ending in -ee are mostly feminine (गाड़ी, लड़की), and the rest must be memorised.

guide.title: His, her, its, their
guide.text:
'His', 'her' and 'its' are one word: उसका (uskaa), or इसका (iskaa) for someone or something close by. 'Their' is उनका (unkaa) or इनका (inkaa); उनका is also the respectful way to say 'his' or 'her' about one person.

Again the ending follows the thing owned: उसका नाम is 'his name' or 'her name' (नाम is masculine); उसकी गाड़ी is 'his car' or 'her car' (गाड़ी is feminine). Hindi does not tell you whether the owner is a he or a she; English does not tell you the gender of the car. Each language marks a different thing.

'Whose' is किसका (kiskaa), with the same endings.

examples.english: What is his name? / What is her name?

guide.title: The Hindi 's: kaa, kee, ke
guide.text:
With a noun, possession is shown by का (kaa) placed after the owner, exactly like English 's: राज का घर, 'Raj's house'. The same word translates 'of': घर का दरवाज़ा, 'the door of the house', literally 'house's door'.

का agrees with the thing owned in the usual way: राज का घर (masculine), राज की गाड़ी (feminine), राज के बच्चे (plural).

का is a postposition, so the owner in front of it takes the oblique form that you will study in the next unit. For now notice one consequence: मेरा भाई ('my brother') becomes मेरे भाई का नाम ('my brother's name'), with मेरे instead of मेरा.

examples.native: मेरे भाई का नाम अमित है।
examples.roman: mere bhaaee kaa naam amit hai.

guide.title: One's own: apnaa
guide.text:
When the owner is the same person as the subject of the sentence, Hindi does not repeat मेरा, आपका or उसका. It uses अपना (apnaa, 'one's own') instead, with the usual endings अपना, अपनी, अपने.

'I am doing my work' is मैं अपना काम कर रहा हूँ, not मैं मेरा काम .... 'Please write your name' is अपना नाम लिखिए.

This removes an ambiguity English has. वह अपनी किताब पढ़ रहा है means he is reading his own book; वह उसकी किताब पढ़ रहा है means he is reading someone else's.

examples.native: मैं अपना काम कर रहा हूँ।
examples.roman: main apnaa kaam kar rahaa hoon.
examples.english: I am doing my work. (man speaking)

examples.native: वह अपनी किताब पढ़ रहा है।
examples.roman: vah apnee kitaab parh rahaa hai.

phrases.note: मेरी because किताब is feminine; it has nothing to do with the speaker's gender.
The same sentence means 'What is her name?'

phrases.english: Where is your phone? (to a friend)

phrases.note: उनका is also the respectful 'his' or 'her' about one person.

phrases.native: मेरे भाई का नाम अमित है।
phrases.roman: mere bhaaee kaa naam amit hai.
phrases.note: मेरा becomes मेरे because भाई is followed by the postposition का.

phrases.native: मेरी माँ का घर दिल्ली में है।
phrases.roman: meree maan kaa ghar dillee mein hai.
phrases.english: My mother's house is in Delhi.
phrases.literal: my mother 's house Delhi in is

phrases.native: मैं अपना काम कर रहा हूँ।
phrases.roman: main apnaa kaam kar rahaa hoon.
phrases.note: A woman says: ... कर रही हूँ (kar rahee hoon). अपना, not मेरा, because the owner is the subject.
A warm thing to say when parting.

units.title: In, on, to, from, with
units.description: Use the little words that follow nouns, and change the noun correctly in front of them.

guide.title: The basic postpositions
guide.text:
Where English puts a preposition before the noun, Hindi puts a postposition after it. The main ones are:

में (mein): in, inside. कमरे में, 'in the room'.
पर (par): on, at. मेज़ पर, 'on the table'; घर पर, 'at home'.
से (se): from; by, with (a means); than. दिल्ली से, 'from Delhi'; बस से, 'by bus'.
को (ko): to; it also marks a specific person as the object of a verb. राज को बुलाइए, 'call Raj'.
तक (tak): up to, until. सोमवार तक, 'until Monday'.
का, की, के (kaa, kee, ke): of, 's.

Note that में (mein, 'in') and मैं (main, 'I') are different words with different vowels.

examples.english: The book is on the table.

guide.title: The oblique: nouns change before a postposition
guide.text:
A noun followed by a postposition takes a special form called the oblique. This is one of the most important rules in Hindi, and forgetting it is the commonest learner's mistake.

Singular: masculine nouns ending in -aa change -aa to -e. कमरा (kamraa, room) becomes कमरे में (kamre mein, in the room); लड़का becomes लड़के को. Other singular nouns, masculine or feminine, do not change: घर में, मेज़ पर, गाड़ी में.

Plural: every noun takes the ending -on (ों). कमरों में (kamron mein, in the rooms), लोगों को (logon ko, to the people), दोस्तों के साथ (doston ke saath, with friends), लड़कियों को (larkiyon ko, to the girls).

Adjectives and possessives in -aa standing before the noun change to -e as well, singular or plural: मेरा बड़ा कमरा becomes मेरे बड़े कमरे में, 'in my big room'.

guide.title: Pronouns before a postposition
guide.text:
Pronouns have oblique forms too, and the postposition is written joined to them.

मैं becomes मुझ: मुझसे (mujhse, from me, with me), मुझको or, far more often, मुझे (mujhe, to me).
तुम stays: तुमसे, तुमको or तुम्हें (tumhen).
आप stays: आपसे, आपको.
हम stays: हमसे, हमको or हमें (hamen).
यह becomes इस and वह becomes उस: इसमें (ismein, in this), उससे (usse, from him or her), उसको or उसे (use, to him or her).
ये becomes इन and वे becomes उन: इनसे, उनको or उन्हें (unhen, to them).
कौन (who) becomes किस: किससे (kisse, with whom), किसको (kisko, to whom).

The short forms मुझे, उसे, हमें, तुम्हें, उन्हें are the ones you will hear all the time.

examples.english: Please talk to me in Hindi.
Please call him. / Please call her.

guide.title: Two-word postpositions with ke
guide.text:
Many relations are expressed by के (ke) plus another word. The noun before के is in the oblique.

के साथ (ke saath): with, together with. के लिए (ke liye): for. के पास (ke paas): near; in the possession of. के बाद (ke baad): after. के ऊपर (ke oopar): above, on top of. के नीचे (ke neeche): under. के अंदर (ke andar): inside. के बाहर (ke baahar): outside. के सामने (ke saamne): in front of, opposite. के पीछे (ke peechhe): behind. A few take की or से instead: की तरफ़ (kee taraf, towards), से पहले (se pahle, before).

With the pronouns मैं, हम, तुम the के merges into the possessive: मेरे साथ (with me), हमारे लिए (for us), तुम्हारे पास (near you). With the others it stays: आपके लिए, उसके साथ, उनके पास.

examples.english: The shop is near the house.
The bag is under the chair.

phrases.english: The book is on the table.

phrases.note: कमरा becomes कमरे before the postposition में.
A woman says: मैं दिल्ली से आई हूँ (... aaee hoon).
A woman says: मैं बस से जाती हूँ (... jaatee hoon).

phrases.english: The shop is near the house.

phrases.note: खाना becomes खाने before के बाद.

phrases.english: Please talk to me in Hindi.
The bag is under the chair.

phrases.note: दोस्त becomes दोस्तों: the oblique plural ending -on.

units.title: Asking questions
units.description: Ask yes-or-no questions and use what, who, where, when, why, how, how many and which.

guide.title: Yes-or-no questions
guide.text:
A statement becomes a yes-or-no question in two ways, and the word order does not change in either.

1. Put क्या (kyaa) at the very beginning. Here क्या is not 'what'; it is only a spoken question mark. आप ठीक हैं is 'you are fine'; क्या आप ठीक हैं? is 'are you fine?'.

2. Just raise your voice at the end: आप ठीक हैं? This is what people mostly do in conversation.

To check that someone agrees, add न (na) at the end, like English 'isn't it?' or 'right?': चाय अच्छी है न?

examples.english: The tea is good, isn't it?

guide.title: The question words
guide.text:
Hindi question words all begin with k, as English ones begin with wh.

क्या (kyaa): what. कौन (kaun): who. कहाँ (kahaan): where. कब (kab): when. क्यों (kyon): why. कैसे (kaise): how. कितना (kitnaa): how much. कौन सा (kaun saa): which. किसका (kiskaa): whose.

The important difference from English is position. The question word does not move to the front. It stays where the answer would be, which normally means just before the verb. 'Where is the market?' is बाज़ार कहाँ है?, 'market where is?', and the answer बाज़ार वहाँ है, 'market there is', has exactly the same shape.

When क्या stands just before the verb it means 'what'; when it opens the sentence it is the yes-or-no marker.

examples.english: When will you come? (to a man)

guide.title: Question words that change their ending
guide.text:
Three question words are adjectives and agree with the noun they refer to, in the usual -aa, -ee, -e pattern.

कैसा, कैसी, कैसे (kaisaa, kaisee, kaise): what kind of, how (is it). कमरा कैसा है? 'How is the room?' चाय कैसी है? 'How is the tea?' The form कैसे is also the adverb 'how, in what way'.

कितना, कितनी, कितने (kitnaa, kitnee, kitne): how much, how many. कितना पानी? 'How much water?' कितनी चीनी? 'How much sugar?' कितने लोग? 'How many people?'

कौन सा, कौन सी, कौन से (kaun saa, kaun see, kaun se): which. कौन सा दिन? 'Which day?' कौन सी किताब? 'Which book?'

guide.title: Who and what before a postposition
guide.text:
Before a postposition, कौन (who) changes to किस (kis), just as वह changes to उस: किससे (kisse, with whom, from whom), किसको (kisko, to whom), किसका (kiskaa, whose), किसके लिए (kiske liye, for whom).

किस is also the oblique of 'which': किस कमरे में? 'In which room?' किस तरफ़? 'In which direction?'

examples.native: आप किससे बात कर रहे हैं?
examples.roman: aap kisse baat kar rahe hain?
examples.english: Who are you talking to? (to a man)

phrases.note: To a woman: आप कब आएँगी? (aap kab aaengee?)
To a woman: ... हँस रही हैं? (hans rahee hain?)

phrases.native: आप किससे बात कर रहे हैं?
phrases.roman: aap kisse baat kar rahe hain?
phrases.note: To a woman: ... कर रही हैं? (kar rahee hain?)

phrases.english: The tea is good, isn't it?

phrases.note: Also the natural way to ask 'What's the matter?'

units.title: Saying no
units.description: Make sentences negative, tell someone not to do something, and say nothing, nobody and never.

guide.title: naheen goes before the verb
guide.text:
To make a sentence negative, put नहीं (naheen) directly before the verb. यह ठीक है, 'this is right', becomes यह ठीक नहीं है, 'this is not right'.

With 'to be', नहीं comes before है, हूँ or हैं. With other verbs it comes before the main verb: मैं नहीं जानता, 'I do not know'.

One special habit: in the present tense the final है, हूँ or हैं is usually dropped in the negative. 'I eat meat' is मैं मांस खाता हूँ, but 'I don't eat meat' is normally just मैं मांस नहीं खाता. Keeping the हूँ is not wrong; it is simply heavier. The है of a plain 'is not' sentence can be dropped in speech too (मुझे नहीं पता, 'I don't know'), but it is safer to keep it there.

guide.title: Don't! uses mat
guide.text:
With commands and requests the negative word is मत (mat), not नहीं. It also goes before the verb: मत जाइए, 'please don't go'; शोर मत करो, 'don't make a noise'.

With the polite -iye form you will also hear and read न (na), which is a little gentler and more formal: न जाइए. On signs you often see it: यहाँ गाड़ी खड़ी न करें, 'do not park here'.

guide.title: Nothing, nobody, never, nowhere
guide.text:
Hindi makes these by pairing an ordinary indefinite word with नहीं. There is no separate word like 'nothing'.

कुछ (kuchh, something) + नहीं: nothing. कोई (koee, someone, any) + नहीं: nobody, none. कभी (kabhee, sometime, ever) + नहीं: never. कहीं (kaheen, somewhere) + नहीं: nowhere.

The two parts may stand together or be separated by other words, with नहीं before the verb as always: मैं कभी देर से नहीं आता, 'I never come late'.

The same indefinite words without नहीं are useful too: कुछ खाइए ('eat something'), कोई है? ('is anyone there?').

examples.native: मैं कभी देर से नहीं आता।
examples.roman: main kabhee der se naheen aataa.

guide.title: Short negative answers
guide.text: A complete sentence is not needed. नहीं on its own is 'no'; with जी it is polite. अभी नहीं (abhee naheen) is 'not now', यहाँ नहीं 'not here', आज नहीं 'not today', मैं नहीं 'not me'. The word नहीं simply follows whatever it denies.

phrases.note: A woman says: मैं नहीं जानती (main naheen jaantee).
A woman says: मैं मांस नहीं खाती (... khaatee). The final हूँ is dropped in the negative.
The same sentence means 'She is not at home'.

phrases.native: मैं कभी देर से नहीं आता।
phrases.roman: main kabhee der se naheen aataa.
phrases.literal: I ever lateness with not coming
phrases.note: A woman says: ... नहीं आती (naheen aatee).
The same for men and women: the verb agrees with हिंदी.
A woman says: मैं नहीं आ सकती (... aa saktee).

units.title: This, that, here, there
units.description: Point things out: this and that, these and those, here and there.

guide.title: This and that, these and those
guide.text:
यह (yah, said 'ye') is 'this' and वह (vah, said 'vo') is 'that'. Their plurals are ये (ye), 'these', and वे (ve), 'those'.

They work both alone and in front of a noun: यह अच्छा है, 'this is good'; यह कमरा अच्छा है, 'this room is good'.

In relaxed speech many people say 'ye' for both यह and ये, and 'vo' for both वह and वे, and let the verb show the number. In writing, and in this course, the four are kept apart.

guide.title: Before a postposition: is, us, in, un
guide.text:
When the noun they point to is followed by a postposition, these words take their oblique forms, just as nouns do.

यह becomes इस (is): इस कमरे में, 'in this room'.
वह becomes उस (us): उस दुकान में, 'in that shop'.
ये becomes इन (in): इन लोगों को, 'to these people'.
वे becomes उन (un): उन दिनों में, 'in those days'.

Used alone as pronouns they join up with the postposition: इसमें ('in this'), उससे ('from that'), इनमें से ('from among these'), and with को the short forms इसे (ise) and उसे (use).

Saying यह कमरे में instead of इस कमरे में is a very common learner's mistake.

guide.title: Here and there
guide.text:
यहाँ (yahaan) is 'here' and वहाँ (vahaan) is 'there'. They need no postposition: यहाँ आइए, 'come here'.

इधर (idhar) and उधर (udhar) mean 'this way, over here' and 'that way, over there'; they suggest a direction or a rough area rather than an exact spot.

Adding the sense of 'right, exactly' gives यहीं (yaheen, 'right here') and वहीं (vaheen, 'right there'). These are यहाँ and वहाँ fused with the emphatic word ही (hee), which you will meet constantly: ऐसा ही, 'just like this'.

examples.english: There is a hotel over there.

guide.title: Like this, this much
guide.text:
Two more pairs follow the same near and far pattern: the near word begins with ऐ or इ, like यह and इधर, and the far word with व or उ, like वह and उधर.

ऐसा (aisaa), 'like this, such', and वैसा (vaisaa), 'like that'. They are adjectives: ऐसा, ऐसी, ऐसे.

इतना (itnaa), 'this much, so much', and उतना (utnaa), 'that much': इतना महँगा!, 'so expensive!'.

And for time: अब (ab), 'now', and तब (tab), 'then'.

examples.english: I want one just like this.

phrases.note: यह becomes इस, and कमरा becomes कमरे, because of में.

phrases.english: There is a hotel over there.
I want one just like this.

units.title: Describing things
units.description: Describe people and things, make adjectives agree, and compare one thing with another.

guide.title: Two kinds of adjective
guide.text:
Adjectives come before the noun, as in English, or before the verb 'to be': बड़ा कमरा, 'a big room'; कमरा बड़ा है, 'the room is big'.

Adjectives whose basic form ends in -aa change to agree with the noun. They end in -aa with a masculine singular noun, -e with a masculine plural noun, and -ee with any feminine noun, singular or plural. So: अच्छा लड़का (a good boy), अच्छे लड़के (good boys), अच्छी लड़की (a good girl), अच्छी लड़कियाँ (good girls).

All other adjectives never change: सुंदर (sundar, beautiful), लाल (laal, red), साफ़ (saaf, clean), खराब (kharaab, bad), ठीक (theek, fine), तैयार (taiyaar, ready). लाल साड़ी, लाल कमरा, लाल गाड़ियाँ: always लाल.

The same -aa, -e, -ee pattern is the one you have already met in मेरा, का, कैसा and कितना, and you will meet it again in verbs. It is the heartbeat of Hindi grammar.

guide.title: Adjectives before a postposition
guide.text:
When a masculine noun is followed by a postposition, an -aa adjective in front of it changes to -e, whether the noun is singular or plural. This is the oblique again.

बड़ा कमरा ('the big room') becomes बड़े कमरे में ('in the big room'). छोटा भाई ('younger brother') becomes छोटे भाई को ('to the younger brother'), even though भाई itself does not change.

Feminine adjectives stay -ee everywhere: छोटी बहन को, 'to the younger sister'.

guide.title: Comparing
guide.text:
Hindi adjectives have no '-er' and '-est' forms. Comparison is done with से (se), which here means 'than'.

The pattern is: A, B से, adjective. राज अमित से बड़ा है, word for word 'Raj Amit than big is', means 'Raj is bigger (or older) than Amit'. The adjective itself does not change its form.

For 'the most', compare with everything: सबसे (sabse, 'than all'). यह सबसे अच्छा है, 'this is the best'.

When nothing is named to compare with, add ज़्यादा (zyaadaa, 'more') or कम (kam, 'less'): यह ज़्यादा महँगा है, 'this one is more expensive'. And इससे (isse, 'than this') is very handy in shops: इससे सस्ता, 'cheaper than this'.

examples.english: I want a cheaper one than this.

guide.title: Very, a little, too
guide.text:
बहुत (bahut) is 'very' and also 'a lot'. थोड़ा (thoraa) is 'a little, slightly'; it agrees like an -aa adjective when it goes with a noun (थोड़ा पानी, थोड़ी चीनी). काफ़ी (kaafee) is 'quite, fairly'.

Hindi has no everyday single word for 'too' in the sense of 'excessively'. बहुत often carries that meaning from context (चाय बहुत मीठी है can be 'the tea is very sweet' or 'too sweet'), and to be explicit people say बहुत ज़्यादा (bahut zyaadaa, 'very much more') or ज़्यादा alone.

phrases.note: लंबा means both 'tall' (of people) and 'long'.
आम has the same form in the plural; the adjective and verb show the number.
लाल never changes its ending.
बड़ा means 'big' and, of people, 'older'.

phrases.english: I want a cheaper one than this.
The new car is very good.
phrases.note: नया (nayaa, new) has the forms नया, नए, नई.
Depending on the tone this can also mean 'too sweet'.

phrases.native: मेरा छोटा भाई दिल्ली में है।
phrases.roman: meraa chhotaa bhaaee dillee mein hai.
phrases.english: My younger brother is in Delhi.
phrases.literal: my small brother Delhi in is

units.title: What you usually do
units.description: Talk about habits, routines and general facts with the everyday present tense.

guide.title: Stem + taa + 'to be'
guide.text:
The dictionary form of every Hindi verb ends in -ना (-naa): करना (karnaa, to do), बोलना (bolnaa, to speak), जाना (jaanaa, to go). Remove -ना and you have the stem: कर, बोल, जा. Everything else is built on the stem.

The everyday present tense has three parts: the stem, the ending -ता (-taa), and the right form of 'to be'. मैं बोलता हूँ, piece by piece 'I speak-ing am', means 'I speak'.

This tense is for what happens regularly or is generally true: 'I speak Hindi', 'I drink tea every day', 'the shop opens at ten'. It is not for what is happening at this moment; that needs the continuous tense of the next unit.

examples.english: I drink tea every day. (man speaking)

guide.title: The ending agrees with the subject
guide.text:
The -ता part is like an -aa adjective and agrees with the subject in gender and number.

-ता (-taa): one male. मैं करता हूँ, वह करता है.
-ते (-te): several males or a mixed group, and always with आप and तुम for a man. हम करते हैं, आप करते हैं, तुम करते हो.
-ती (-tee): any female subject, one or many. मैं करती हूँ, वह करती है, आप करती हैं, वे करती हैं.

The form of 'to be' agrees with the person as usual: हूँ with मैं, हो with तुम, है with one he, she or it, हैं with हम, आप and they.

A thing counts as male or female according to the gender of its noun: बस (bus) and दुकान (shop) are feminine, so यह बस कहाँ जाती है? and दुकान दस बजे खुलती है.

Remember respect: of your mother you say मेरी माँ खाना बनाती हैं, with plural हैं.

examples.english: Where do you work? (to a man)
The children play in the evening.

guide.title: Questions and negatives
guide.text:
Questions need no helping verb like English 'do'. Use क्या at the front, or a question word before the verb: क्या आप मांस खाते हैं? 'Do you eat meat?'

In the negative, नहीं goes before the verb and the final हूँ, है or हैं is normally left out: मैं कॉफ़ी नहीं पीता, 'I don't drink coffee'. There is one detail to notice: when a feminine plural verb loses its हैं, the nasal moves onto the verb, so वे नहीं जातीं (jaateen), 'they (women) don't go'.

examples.english: Do you eat meat? (to a man)

guide.title: Words for how often
guide.text:
Habit sentences often contain a time word. These go early in the sentence, usually right after the subject.

रोज़ (roz): every day. हर (har): every, as in हर रविवार, 'every Sunday'. हमेशा (hameshaa): always. कभी-कभी (kabhee-kabhee): sometimes. अक्सर (aksar): often. सुबह (subah): in the morning. शाम को (shaam ko): in the evening. रात को (raat ko): at night. जल्दी (jaldee): early, quickly.

examples.english: I get up early in the morning. (man speaking)

examples.native: वे हर रविवार मंदिर जाते हैं।
examples.roman: ve har ravivaar mandir jaate hain.
examples.english: They go to the temple every Sunday.
The shop opens at ten o'clock.

phrases.note: A woman says: मैं हिंदी बोलती हूँ (... boltee hoon).
To a woman: ... काम करती हैं? (kaam kartee hain?)
A woman says: ... पीती हूँ (peetee hoon).
'He goes to school' is वह स्कूल जाता है (vah skool jaataa hai).
A group of women only: ... रहती हैं (rahtee hain).

phrases.english: The children play in the evening.
I get up early in the morning.
phrases.note: A woman says: ... उठती हूँ (uthtee hoon).
To a woman: ... खाती हैं? (khaatee hain?)
बस is feminine, so जाती.
Plural हैं out of respect for one's mother.

phrases.english: The shop opens at ten o'clock.

phrases.note: A woman says: ... पढ़ाती हूँ (parhaatee hoon). Compare पढ़ना (to study, to read) with पढ़ाना (to teach).

phrases.native: वे हर रविवार मंदिर जाते हैं।
phrases.roman: ve har ravivaar mandir jaate hain.
phrases.english: They go to the temple every Sunday.
phrases.literal: they every Sunday temple going are

phrases.note: A woman says: ... नहीं पीती (naheen peetee).

units.title: Happening now
units.description: Say what is happening at this moment, and what was happening at some moment in the past.

guide.title: Stem + rahaa + 'to be'
guide.text:
For an action in progress Hindi uses three separate words: the bare stem of the verb, then रहा (rahaa), then the present of 'to be'. मैं खा रहा हूँ, piece by piece 'I eat staying am', means 'I am eating'.

रहा is the part that agrees with the subject: रहा (rahaa) for one male, रहे (rahe) for males in the plural and for आप and तुम addressed to a man, रही (rahee) for any female subject.

The stem never changes. So once you know रहा, रहे, रही and the forms of 'to be', you can put any verb into this tense: कर रहा हूँ (am doing), जा रही है (she is going), आ रहे हैं (are coming).

examples.english: What are you doing? (to a man)

guide.title: Things that happen by themselves
guide.text:
Weather, noises and many other events are expressed with a noun plus होना (to be, to happen) or another simple verb, and the verb agrees with that noun.

बारिश (rain) is feminine: बारिश हो रही है, 'rain is happening', that is, 'it is raining'. फ़ोन is masculine: फ़ोन बज रहा है, 'the phone is ringing'.

A very large number of Hindi verbs are made this way, from a noun or adjective plus करना (to do) or होना (to happen): बात करना ('to do talk', to talk), इंतज़ार करना (to wait), काम करना (to work). In the continuous they simply become बात कर रहे हैं, इंतज़ार कर रहा हूँ.

examples.native: हम आपका इंतज़ार कर रहे हैं।
examples.roman: ham aapkaa intazaar kar rahe hain.

guide.title: Was doing; and 'I am going tomorrow'
guide.text:
Replace the present of 'to be' with था, थी, थे, थीं and you have the past continuous: मैं सो रहा था, 'I was sleeping'; वह सो रही थी, 'she was sleeping'.

As in English, the present continuous is also used for a firm plan in the near future: मैं कल दिल्ली जा रहा हूँ, 'I am going to Delhi tomorrow'.

The negative keeps the helping verb more often than the habitual tense does: मैं नहीं जा रहा हूँ or मैं नहीं जा रहा, 'I am not going'.

examples.native: मैं कल दिल्ली जा रहा हूँ।
examples.roman: main kal dillee jaa rahaa hoon.
examples.english: I am going to Delhi tomorrow. (man speaking)

guide.title: A trap: sitting, standing, wearing
guide.text:
English says 'he is sitting' for someone who is already seated. Hindi sees that as a state, not an action in progress, and uses a different form: वह बैठा है (vah baithaa hai), literally 'he is seated'. वह बैठ रहा है would mean that he is in the act of lowering himself onto the chair.

The same goes for standing (वह खड़ा है, 'he is standing'), lying down, and wearing clothes. Keep the continuous for real ongoing activity.

phrases.note: A woman says: ... खा रही हूँ (khaa rahee hoon).
To a woman: ... कर रही हैं? (kar rahee hain?)
'He is sleeping' is वह सो रहा है (vah so rahaa hai).
A woman says: मैं आ रही हूँ (main aa rahee hoon).

phrases.native: हम आपका इंतज़ार कर रहे हैं।
phrases.roman: ham aapkaa intazaar kar rahe hain.

phrases.note: To a woman: ... जा रही हैं? (jaa rahee hain?)
A woman says: ... पढ़ रही हूँ (parh rahee hoon).
Of a woman: वह क्या कह रही है? (vah kyaa kah rahee hai?)
A woman says: मैं सो रही थी (main so rahee thee).

phrases.native: मैं कल दिल्ली जा रहा हूँ।
phrases.roman: main kal dillee jaa rahaa hoon.
phrases.english: I am going to Delhi tomorrow.
phrases.note: A woman says: ... जा रही हूँ (jaa rahee hoon).

units.title: What happened
units.description: Talk about completed actions in the past, including the special 'ne' sentence pattern.

guide.title: The past form of the verb
guide.text:
The simple past is one word, made from the stem plus an ending that works like an -aa adjective: -आ (-aa) masculine singular, -ए (-e) masculine plural, -ई (-ee) feminine singular, -ईं (-een) feminine plural.

From बोलना (to speak): बोला, बोले, बोली, बोलीं. From देखना (to see): देखा, देखे, देखी, देखीं.

If the stem ends in a vowel, a य (y) is slipped in before -aa: आना (to come) gives आया, आए, आई, आईं; खाना (to eat) gives खाया, खाए, खाई, खाईं.

Six very common verbs are irregular and must be memorised:
जाना (to go): गया, गए, गई, गईं.
करना (to do): किया, किए, की, कीं.
लेना (to take): लिया, लिए, ली, लीं.
देना (to give): दिया, दिए, दी, दीं.
पीना (to drink): पिया, पिए, पी, पीं.
होना (to be, to happen): हुआ, हुए, हुई, हुईं.

examples.native: हम कल रात देर से आए।
examples.roman: ham kal raat der se aae.

guide.title: Verbs without an object agree with the subject
guide.text:
Verbs of movement and other verbs that cannot take a direct object (go, come, arrive, get up, sit, sleep, stay, be) are simple: the past form agrees with the subject, as you would expect.

A man says मैं गया ('I went'), a woman says मैं गई. To a man you say आप कब आए?, to a woman आप कब आईं?

examples.english: I went to the market yesterday. (man speaking)
I went to the market yesterday. (woman speaking)
When did you come? (to a man)

guide.title: Verbs with an object: the ne pattern
guide.text:
This is the most unusual rule in Hindi, so take it slowly. With verbs that take a direct object (eat, drink, see, do, give, buy, say, read, write and so on), in the simple past and the tenses built on it:

1. The doer is followed by ने (ne).
2. The verb does NOT agree with the doer. It agrees with the object, the thing eaten, seen or bought.

'I ate the food' is मैंने खाना खाया. खाया is masculine because खाना (food) is masculine. 'I drank tea' is मैंने चाय पी, with feminine पी because चाय is feminine. It makes no difference whether the speaker is a man or a woman.

The pronouns with ने are: मैंने (mainne), तुमने (tumne), आपने (aapne), हमने (hamne), उसने (usne, he or she), उन्होंने (unhonne, they, or he or she with respect), किसने (kisne, who?). A noun before ने takes the oblique: लड़के ने, बच्चों ने.

3. If the object is marked with को (as specific people usually are), or if there is no object to agree with, the verb stays in the neutral masculine singular: मैंने राज को देखा, 'I saw Raj'; मैंने सीता को देखा, 'I saw Sita'.

A few verbs take an object and still do not use ने, notably लाना (to bring) and भूलना (to forget), while बोलना (to speak) is normally used without it: वह कुछ नहीं बोला, 'he said nothing'.

examples.english: He gave me a book. / She gave me a book.

guide.title: Have done, had done, used to do
guide.text:
Add the present of 'to be' to the past form and you get 'have done': मैंने यह फ़िल्म देखी है, 'I have seen this film'; वह अभी गई है, 'she has just left'. The ने rule stays exactly the same.

Add था, थी, थे instead and you get 'had done', which Hindi also uses for a plain past event that is over and done with: मैं कल आया था, 'I came yesterday'.

For what used to happen regularly, use the habitual form with था: मैं पहले यहाँ रहता था, 'I used to live here before'. There is no ने in this tense, because it is not built on the past form.

In the negative, नहीं goes before the verb as always: मैंने नहीं देखा, 'I didn't see (it)'.

examples.english: I used to live here before. (man speaking)

phrases.english: I went to the market yesterday.
phrases.note: A woman says: मैं कल बाज़ार गई (... gaee).
The same for men and women: the verb agrees with खाना (masculine), not with the speaker.
पी is feminine to agree with चाय.
The same sentence means 'She gave me a book'. दी is feminine to agree with किताब.

phrases.native: हम कल रात देर से आए।
phrases.roman: ham kal raat der se aae.
phrases.literal: we yesterday night lateness with came

phrases.note: 'He has just left' is वह अभी गया है (vah abhee gayaa hai).
खरीदीं is feminine plural to agree with किताबें.

phrases.english: I used to live here before.
phrases.note: A woman says: ... रहती थी (rahtee thee).
Also 'He helped me' or 'She helped me' said with respect. की is feminine to agree with मदद.
Because the object has को, the verb stays in the neutral form देखा.
A woman says: ... पहुँची (pahunchee). No ने: 'arrive' has no object.

units.title: What will happen
units.description: Talk about plans and predictions, make offers and suggest doing something together.

guide.title: The future endings
guide.text:
The future is one word: the stem, an ending for the person, and then -गा (-gaa), -गे (-ge) or -गी (-gee) for gender and number. Taking करना (to do):

मैं करूँगा (karoongaa): I will do. A woman says करूँगी (karoongee).
तुम करोगे (karoge): you will do, to a friend. To a woman, करोगी.
यह, वह करेगा (karegaa): he or it will do; करेगी, she will do. The intimate तू takes this form too.
हम, आप, वे करेंगे (karenge): we, you (polite), they will do. For women only, करेंगी (karengee).

The middle of the word is nasal for 'I' (-oon-) and for the plural (-en-); the singular करेगा has no nasal. Listen for the difference between आएगा (he will come) and आएँगे (they or you will come).

After a stem ending in a vowel the endings are written as separate vowel letters: जाना gives जाऊँगा, जाओगे, जाएगा, जाएँगे; आना gives आऊँगा, आओगे, आएगा, आएँगे.

examples.english: What will you do? (to a male friend)
He will come in the evening.
When will you go? (to a man)

guide.title: Three irregular verbs
guide.text:
लेना (to take), देना (to give) and होना (to be) shorten their stems in the future.

लेना: लूँगा (loongaa), लोगे, लेगा, लेंगे (lenge).
देना: दूँगा (doongaa), दोगे, देगा, देंगे (denge).
होना: हूँगा (hoongaa), होगे, होगा (hogaa), होंगे (honge).

लेना is the polite verb for accepting food and drink: क्या आप चाय लेंगे? 'Will you have tea?'

Things and events take the gender of their noun: बारिश होगी ('it will rain', बारिश is feminine), ट्रेन कब आएगी? ('when will the train come?').

examples.english: Will you have tea? (to a man)
I will let you know. (man speaking)

guide.title: hogaa for a guess
guide.text:
The future of 'to be' is also used for a guess about the present, like English 'he will be at home by now' or 'he must be at home': वह घर पर होगा.

With another verb it expresses 'must be doing' or 'must have done': वह सो रहा होगा, 'he must be sleeping'. You do not need to produce this yet, but you will hear it often.

guide.title: Shall we?
guide.text:
Take the future form and remove the final -गा, -गे, -गी: what is left is the subjunctive, used for suggestions, permission and possibilities. चलेंगे ('we will go') becomes चलें? ('shall we go?'); मैं आऊँगा ('I will come') becomes मैं आऊँ? ('may I come? shall I come?').

It is one of the politest and most useful forms in the language: क्या मैं अंदर आऊँ? 'May I come in?' कहाँ बैठें? 'Where shall we sit?'

Negative future sentences simply put नहीं before the verb: मैं नहीं आऊँगा, 'I will not come'.

examples.english: Shall I come? / May I come?

phrases.note: A woman says: ... करूँगी (karoongee).
To a woman: आप कब जाएँगी? (aap kab jaaengee?)

phrases.english: He will come in the evening.
phrases.note: 'She will come' is वह शाम को आएगी (... aaegee).
To a woman: ... लेंगी? (lengee?)
A woman says: ... बता दूँगी (bataa doongee).
ट्रेन is feminine, so आएगी.

phrases.english: What will you do? (to a friend)
phrases.note: To a female friend: तुम क्या करोगी? (tum kyaa karogee?)
The future of 'to be' expresses a guess about the present.
A woman says: ... आऊँगी (aaoongee).

units.title: Requests and commands
units.description: Ask people to do things, politely or casually, and tell them not to.

guide.title: Three levels, three endings
guide.text:
The form of a request matches the word for 'you' that you would use to that person.

With आप, add -इए (-iye) to the stem: बैठिए (baithiye, please sit), आइए (aaiye, please come), बताइए (bataaiye, please tell). This is the form to use by default; it already contains the 'please'.

With तुम, add -ओ (-o): बैठो (baitho), आओ (aao), बताओ (bataao). This is for friends, children and younger relatives. It is friendly, not rude, in the right company.

With तू, use the bare stem: बैठ, आ, बता. Intimate or rough; recognise it only.

The word for 'you' is normally left out, exactly as in English.

examples.english: Come here. (to a friend or child)
Hurry up. (to a friend or child)

guide.title: Four irregular polite forms
guide.text:
Four everyday verbs have irregular forms with आप, all ending in -ीजिए (-eejiye):

करना (to do): कीजिए (keejiye). With तुम: करो.
देना (to give): दीजिए (deejiye). With तुम: दो.
लेना (to take): लीजिए (leejiye). With तुम: लो.
पीना (to drink): पीजिए (peejiye). With तुम: पियो.

Because so many Hindi verbs are made of a noun plus करना, the word कीजिए turns up everywhere: बंद कीजिए (please close), माफ़ कीजिए (please forgive), इंतज़ार कीजिए (please wait).

In everyday speech you will also hear करिए (kariye) for कीजिए; both are understood, but कीजिए is the standard form.

guide.title: Don't, and softer requests
guide.text:
For 'don't', put मत (mat) before the verb at any level: मत जाइए, शोर मत करो.

To soften a request, begin with ज़रा (zaraa, 'just'): ज़रा रुकिए, 'just wait a moment, please'. Adding a helper verb such as दीजिए after the stem also makes a request sound more considerate: खोलिए is 'open', खिड़की खोल दीजिए is closer to 'would you open the window'. Helper verbs have their own unit later.

For an especially courteous request, particularly one to be carried out later, add -गा to the polite form: आइएगा (aaiyegaa), 'do please come'.

examples.english: Don't make a noise. (to a friend or child)

guide.title: Let's go; and the infinitive as a command
guide.text:
चलिए (chaliye) and, to friends, चलो (chalo) literally mean 'walk, move', but they are the standard way to say 'come on' and 'let's go'. चलिए, चलते हैं is 'come on, let's go', and चलो is also used like 'right then' or 'okay' to close a topic.

The dictionary form in -ना can be used as a command to people you call तुम. It is neutral in tone and usually refers to something to be done later rather than this second: मुझे फ़ोन करना, 'call me (sometime)'; भूलना मत, 'don't forget'.

examples.english: Call me. (to a friend, later on)

phrases.note: Said when handing something over, like 'here you are'.

phrases.english: Come here. (to a friend or child)
Hurry up. (to a friend or child)
phrases.note: Polite: जल्दी कीजिए (jaldee keejiye).

phrases.english: Call me. (to a friend, later on)
phrases.note: The -naa form as a relaxed instruction for later.

phrases.english: Don't make a noise. (to a friend or child)

phrases.note: The ending -iyegaa is an extra-courteous request, often an invitation.

units.title: Want, need, can, must
units.description: Say what you want, what you need, what you are able to do and what you have to do.

guide.title: Wanting a thing: chaahiye
guide.text:
To say you want or need a thing, Hindi turns the sentence round: the thing is wanted 'to' you. मुझे पानी चाहिए, word for word 'to-me water is-wanted', covers both 'I want water' and 'I need water'.

The person is in the 'to' form: मुझे (to me), हमें (to us), तुम्हें (to you, familiar), आपको (to you, polite), उसे (to him, to her), उन्हें (to them). A noun takes को: राज को पानी चाहिए.

चाहिए itself does not change for person. It is always चाहिए with one thing; with several things careful speakers write चाहिएँ, but in speech you will mostly hear चाहिए for both.

The negative is नहीं चाहिए: मुझे नहीं चाहिए, 'I don't want it'.

guide.title: Wanting to do something: chaahnaa
guide.text:
To want to DO something, use the ordinary verb चाहना (chaahnaa, to want) after the -ना form of the other verb. The subject is the normal मैं, आप and so on, and चाहना is conjugated like any verb.

मैं हिंदी सीखना चाहता हूँ, 'I Hindi to-learn wanting am', is 'I want to learn Hindi'. A woman says चाहती हूँ.

This sounds quite direct. When asking for something politely, मुझे ... चाहिए or a request in -इए is usually better than मैं ... चाहता हूँ.

examples.english: I want to learn Hindi. (man speaking)
What do you want to eat? (to a man)

guide.title: Can: saknaa
guide.text:
'Can' is सकना (saknaa). It never stands alone; it follows the bare stem of the main verb and takes all the endings itself: मैं आ सकता हूँ ('I can come'), वह पढ़ सकती है ('she can read'), हम जा सकते हैं ('we can go').

It covers ability, possibility and permission, like English 'can': क्या मैं अंदर आ सकता हूँ? 'May I come in?' क्या आप मेरी मदद कर सकते हैं? 'Can you help me?'

In the negative, नहीं usually goes before the stem and the final हूँ, है is dropped: मैं नहीं आ सकता, 'I can't come'.

For a skill that you have learnt, such as a language, swimming or driving, Hindi prefers the 'comes to me' pattern: मुझे हिंदी आती है, 'I know Hindi'.

examples.native: क्या मैं अंदर आ सकता हूँ?
examples.roman: kyaa main andar aa saktaa hoon?

examples.native: क्या आप धीरे बोल सकते हैं?
examples.roman: kyaa aap dheere bol sakte hain?
examples.english: Can you speak slowly? (to a man)

guide.title: Have to, will have to, should
guide.text:
Obligation again uses the 'to me' pattern, with the -ना form of the verb. There are three strengths.

-ना + है: something you are due to do, or mean to do. मुझे अब जाना है, 'I have to go now'. This is also the usual way to say where you want to go: मुझे स्टेशन जाना है.

-ना + पड़ेगा (paregaa, 'will fall'): you are forced to, like it or not. मुझे कल काम करना पड़ेगा, 'I will have to work tomorrow'. In the present, पड़ता है: मुझे रोज़ जाना पड़ता है, 'I have to go every day'.

-ना + चाहिए: you ought to. आपको आराम करना चाहिए, 'you should rest'.

One refinement: when the verb has an object, the -ना form agrees with it like an adjective. दवा (medicine) is feminine, so 'I have to take medicine' is मुझे दवा लेनी है, with लेनी rather than लेना, and 'I will have to take medicine' is मुझे दवा लेनी पड़ेगी.

examples.english: I will have to work tomorrow.

phrases.note: A woman says: ... सीखना चाहती हूँ (seekhnaa chaahtee hoon).

phrases.english: What do you want to eat?
phrases.note: To a woman: ... चाहती हैं? (chaahtee hain?)

phrases.native: क्या मैं अंदर आ सकता हूँ?
phrases.roman: kyaa main andar aa saktaa hoon?
phrases.note: A woman says: ... आ सकती हूँ? (aa saktee hoon?)

phrases.native: क्या आप मेरी मदद कर सकते हैं?
phrases.roman: kyaa aap meree madad kar sakte hain?
phrases.literal: (question) you my help do can are
phrases.note: To a woman: ... कर सकती हैं? (kar saktee hain?)
A woman says: ... पढ़ सकती हूँ (parh saktee hoon).

phrases.native: क्या आप धीरे बोल सकते हैं?
phrases.roman: kyaa aap dheere bol sakte hain?
phrases.note: To a woman: ... बोल सकती हैं? (bol saktee hain?)
A woman says: ... नहीं आ सकती (naheen aa saktee).

phrases.english: I will have to work tomorrow.

phrases.note: लेनी, not लेना, because दवा is feminine.

units.title: Have and have not
units.description: Say what you have, in the three different ways Hindi uses for things, relatives and feelings.

guide.title: Things you own or carry: ke paas
guide.text:
Hindi has no verb 'to have'. Instead it says that something 'is' in some relation to you, and the relation depends on what kind of thing it is.

For objects you own or have with you (a car, money, a pen, a ticket, a phone) and also for time, use के पास (ke paas, 'near'): मेरे पास गाड़ी है, word for word 'near me a car is', means 'I have a car'.

The owner takes the possessive form before पास: मेरे पास (I have), हमारे पास (we have), तुम्हारे पास (you have, familiar), आपके पास (you have, polite), उसके पास (he or she has), उनके पास (they have), राज के पास (Raj has).

The verb agrees with the thing possessed: है for one thing, हैं for several. पैसे (money) is plural in Hindi, so मेरे पास पैसे नहीं हैं.

examples.english: He has no money. / She has no money.

guide.title: Relatives and parts of the body: the possessive
guide.text:
You do not 'have' your brother near you like a pen. For family members, friends and parts of your own body, Hindi uses the plain possessive with 'to be': मेरा एक भाई है, 'my one brother is', means 'I have a brother'.

The possessive agrees with the relative in the usual way: मेरा एक बेटा है (I have a son), मेरी दो बहनें हैं (I have two sisters), मेरे दो भाई हैं (I have two brothers), उनके तीन बच्चे हैं (they have three children).

Many speakers use the unchanging form मेरे for all relatives (मेरे एक भाई है); you will hear both.

guide.title: Illnesses, feelings and things to do: ko
guide.text:
What happens to you or is felt by you (a fever, a headache, a cold, hurry, hope, worry, work to be done) is 'to' you, with the same forms as with चाहिए: मुझे, हमें, आपको, उसे, उन्हें.

मुझे बुखार है, 'to me fever is', means 'I have a fever'. मुझे जल्दी है, 'to me hurry is', means 'I am in a hurry'. मुझे एक काम है, 'I have something to do'.

guide.title: There is, there are
guide.text:
'There is' needs no special word. Say where, then what, then है or हैं: यहाँ एक अच्छा होटल है, 'here a good hotel is', means 'there is a good hotel here'. कमरे में पंखा नहीं है, 'there is no fan in the room'.

The difference from 'the hotel is here' lies only in the order: होटल यहाँ है. What is already known comes first; the new information comes just before the verb.

examples.english: There is a good hotel here.
There is no fan in the room.

phrases.note: The same sentence means 'She has no money'. पैसे is plural, so हैं.

phrases.english: How much money do you have?

phrases.native: क्या आपके पास खुले पैसे हैं?
phrases.roman: kyaa aapke paas khule paise hain?
phrases.note: Small change is खुले पैसे (khule paise) or छुट्टे (chhutte).

phrases.english: There is a good hotel here.
There is no fan in the room.

units.title: Helper verbs
units.description: Understand and use the two-verb combinations that make Hindi sound natural.

guide.title: What a compound verb is
guide.text:
Listen to any Hindi conversation and you will notice that verbs come in pairs: बैठ जाइए, खा लिया, बता दीजिए. The first verb, in its bare stem form, carries the meaning. The second is a helper: it loses its own meaning ('go', 'take', 'give'), takes all the endings, and adds a shade of meaning, most often that the action is done completely, once, with a result.

बैठिए and बैठ जाइए both mean 'please sit', but the second is what people actually say: 'do sit down'. मैंने खाया is 'I ate'; मैंने खा लिया is 'I have eaten, I'm done'.

You will be understood without helpers, so treat this unit first as a key to understanding what you hear, and then start copying the commonest pairs as fixed phrases.

guide.title: jaanaa: a change that is complete
guide.text:
जाना ('to go') as a helper goes with verbs that have no object: verbs of movement and of changing state. It shows that the change has fully happened.

आ जाना (to arrive, to come over), बैठ जाना (to sit down), सो जाना (to fall asleep), हो जाना (to become, to get done), भूल जाना (to forget), समझ जाना (to grasp, to get it), निकल जाना (to leave, to slip away).

The helper takes the endings, so it agrees with the subject and there is no ने: वह सो गया ('he fell asleep'), वह सो गई ('she fell asleep'), काम हो गया ('the work is done').

guide.title: lenaa and denaa: for yourself or for someone else
guide.text:
लेना ('to take') as a helper suggests that the action is done for the doer's own benefit, or is taken in: खा लेना (to eat up), पी लेना (to drink up), रख लेना (to keep for oneself), पढ़ लेना (to read through), कर लेना (to get something done).

देना ('to give') suggests that the action is directed away, for someone else's benefit: बता देना (to tell someone), खोल देना (to open for someone), भेज देना (to send off), कर देना (to do for someone), दे देना (to give away, to hand over).

So यह रख लीजिए is 'please keep this (for yourself)', while यह वहाँ रख दीजिए is 'please put this over there (for me)'.

Both helpers take ने in the past, since they are verbs with objects: मैंने उसे पैसे दे दिए, 'I gave him the money'.

guide.title: Already, begin to, manage to
guide.text:
Three more helpers have clearer meanings of their own.

चुकना (chuknaa) after the stem means 'already, to have finished': मैं खा चुका हूँ, 'I have already eaten'. It never takes ने.

लगना (lagnaa) after the -ने form of a verb means 'to begin to': बारिश होने लगी, 'it began to rain'; वह हँसने लगा, 'he started laughing'.

पाना (paanaa) after the stem means 'to manage to, to be able to', and is used mostly in the negative: मैं नहीं आ पाया, 'I couldn't make it'.

One rule of thumb: the helpers जाना, लेना and देना are normally dropped in negative sentences. 'I have eaten' is मैंने खा लिया, but 'I haven't eaten' is simply मैंने नहीं खाया.

phrases.note: A woman says: मैं भूल गई (main bhool gaee).
The same for men and women; लिया agrees with खाना.
'She fell asleep' is वह सो गई (vah so gaee).
A woman says: मैं समझ गई (main samajh gaee).
A woman says: मैं खा चुकी हूँ (main khaa chukee hoon).
Polite: आ जाइए (aa jaaiye).
Also 'I gave her the money'. दिए is plural to agree with पैसे.
A woman says: मैं नहीं आ पाई (main naheen aa paaee).

units.title: Food & drink
units.description: Order food and drink, say what you do and don't eat, and ask for the bill.

guide.title: Ordering
guide.text:
The simplest order is the thing you want followed by दीजिए (deejiye, 'please give'): एक चाय दीजिए, 'one tea, please'. The -इए ending already makes it polite, so no extra word for 'please' is needed.

For 'more' or 'another', put और (aur) after the item: एक रोटी और दीजिए, 'one more roti, please'. और before a noun means 'more' as well: और पानी, 'more water'. When you have had enough, say बस (bas), 'enough, that's all'.

Other useful request verbs: लाइए (laaiye, 'please bring'), ले आइए (le aaiye, 'please bring over'), दिखाइए (dikhaaiye, 'please show').

A waiter is addressed as भैया (bhaiyaa) or simply with सुनिए.

examples.english: That's enough, I don't want any more.

guide.title: Hunger and thirst strike you
guide.text:
You are not hungry in Hindi; hunger 'has attached itself' to you. मुझे भूख लगी है, word for word 'to me hunger has struck', and likewise मुझे प्यास लगी है for thirst. भूख (bhookh) and प्यास (pyaas) are both feminine, which is why the verb is लगी.

The verb लगना (lagnaa), 'to attach, to strike, to feel', is one of the busiest in Hindi. You will meet it again for feeling cold, for how something seems to you, and for how long something takes.

guide.title: Saying what you eat
guide.text:
Many Indians are vegetarian, and restaurants are often marked 'veg' or 'non-veg'. शाकाहारी (shaakaahaaree) is 'vegetarian' and मांसाहारी (maansaahaaree) is 'meat-eating'; in everyday speech the English 'veg' and 'non-veg' are just as common.

To check what is in a dish, use इसमें (ismein, 'in this'): क्या इसमें मांस है? 'Is there meat in this?' Replace मांस with अंडा (andaa, egg), दूध (doodh, milk) or मूँगफली (moongphalee, peanuts) as needed.

For spice, मिर्च (mirch) is chilli and तीखा (teekhaa) is 'hot, spicy'. मिर्च कम डालिए, 'put less chilli', is the request to remember.

guide.title: Words on every menu
guide.text:
A few words will carry you through most meals: रोटी (rotee, flat bread), चावल (chaaval, rice), दाल (daal, lentils), सब्ज़ी (sabzee, vegetables or a vegetable dish), दही (dahee, yoghurt), दूध (doodh, milk), चीनी (cheenee, sugar), नमक (namak, salt), पानी (paanee, water).

Tastes: मीठा (meethaa, sweet), नमकीन (namkeen, salty, savoury), खट्टा (khattaa, sour), कड़वा (karvaa, bitter), तीखा (teekhaa, spicy hot), स्वादिष्ट (svaadisht, delicious).

Tea is normally made with milk and sugar boiled in. If you want it otherwise, say so when ordering.

examples.english: Don't put sugar in the tea.

phrases.note: The -iye verb ending already makes the request polite.
People also simply say 'veg': मैं वेज हूँ (main vej hoon).

phrases.english: Don't put sugar in the tea.

phrases.note: यह is written 'yah' but usually pronounced 'ye'.

phrases.english: That's enough, I don't want any more.

phrases.note: A common friendly question, almost a greeting.

units.title: Directions & getting around
units.description: Ask the way, understand the answer and tell a driver where to go and where to stop.

guide.title: Where is it? How far?
guide.text:
To ask where something is, name it and add कहाँ है? (kahaan hai?): अस्पताल कहाँ है? 'Where is the hospital?' To start politely, open with सुनिए or भैया.

For distance: कितनी दूर है? (kitnee door hai?), 'how far is it?'. दूर (door) is 'far' and पास (paas) or पास में is 'near'. यहाँ से (yahaan se) is 'from here'.

Answers you are likely to hear: बहुत पास है ('it's very near'), थोड़ा दूर है ('it's a bit far'), पाँच मिनट का रास्ता है ('it's a five-minute trip'), पैदल जा सकते हैं ('you can go on foot').

examples.english: How far is it from here?

guide.title: Left, right, straight
guide.text:
The direction words are सीधे (seedhe, straight), बाएँ (baaen, left), दाएँ (daaen, right), आगे (aage, ahead, further on), पीछे (peechhe, behind, back), सामने (saamne, in front, opposite).
