मुड़ना (murnaa) is 'to turn': बाएँ मुड़िए, 'turn left'. People also say बाएँ हाथ and दाएँ हाथ ('left hand', 'right hand') for 'on the left', 'on the right', and in everyday speech you will often hear the English words 'left' and 'right': लेफ़्ट लीजिए, 'take a left'.

की तरफ़ (kee taraf) means 'towards, in the direction of': स्टेशन की तरफ़, 'towards the station'. किस तरफ़? is 'which way?'.

examples.english: Which way is the metro station?

guide.title: Saying where you want to go
guide.text:
Use the 'to me' pattern with जाना है: मुझे स्टेशन जाना है, 'I need to go to the station'.

Notice that there is no word for 'to' before the destination. With verbs of going, the place stands alone. But it is still treated as if a postposition followed, so a masculine noun in -aa takes its oblique -e: हवाई अड्डा (airport) becomes मुझे हवाई अड्डे जाना है.

To ask whether a bus or train goes somewhere: क्या यह बस स्टेशन जाती है?

examples.english: I need to go to the airport.

examples.native: क्या यह बस स्टेशन जाती है?
examples.roman: kyaa yah bas steshan jaatee hai?
examples.english: Does this bus go to the station?
I need to go to the market.

guide.title: Taxis and auto-rickshaws
guide.text:
With a driver you need only a handful of verbs. चलिए (chaliye) is 'let's go, drive on': स्टेशन चलिए, 'to the station, please'. रोकिए (rokiye) or रोक दीजिए is 'stop (the vehicle)': यहाँ रोक दीजिए, 'please stop here'. रुकिए (rukiye) is 'wait'.

Agree on the fare before setting off, or ask for the meter: मीटर से चलिए, 'go by the meter'. किराया (kiraayaa) is the fare; कितना किराया लगेगा?, 'how much will the fare be?', uses लगना again, here in the sense of 'to cost'.

examples.english: How much will the fare be?

phrases.english: How far is it from here?

phrases.note: 'kyaa' at the start turns a statement into a yes/no question.

phrases.english: Which way is the metro station?
I need to go to the airport.
phrases.note: The English word 'airport' (एयरपोर्ट) is equally common.

phrases.native: क्या यह बस स्टेशन जाती है?
phrases.roman: kyaa yah bas steshan jaatee hai?
phrases.english: Does this bus go to the station?
How much will the fare be?

phrases.note: Said to a taxi or auto-rickshaw driver.
Said to a driver.
In cities people often say 'toilet' or 'washroom kahaan hai?'
A woman says: मैं रास्ता भूल गई हूँ (... bhool gaee hoon).

units.title: Shopping, money and bigger numbers
units.description: Ask prices, understand numbers up to a hundred and beyond, bargain and pay.

guide.title: Asking the price
guide.text:
The standard question is यह कितने का है? (yah kitne kaa hai?), literally 'this is of how many (rupees)?'. The का agrees with the thing: कितने का for a masculine item, कितने की for a feminine one (यह साड़ी कितने की है?), कितने के for several.

You can also ask कितने में? ('for how much?'), or use the nouns दाम (daam) and कीमत (keemat), both 'price': इसका दाम क्या है?

The currency is the rupee: एक रुपया (ek rupayaa), 'one rupee'; दो रुपये (do rupaye), 'two rupees', also spelt रुपए. Prices by weight are given as 'fifty rupees kilo': पचास रुपये किलो. To offer a price, use में: सौ रुपये में दीजिए, 'give it for a hundred rupees'.

guide.title: Eleven to twenty
guide.text:
The teens are single words that have to be learnt: ग्यारह (gyaarah, 11), बारह (baarah, 12), तेरह (terah, 13), चौदह (chaudah, 14), पंद्रह (pandrah, 15), सोलह (solah, 16), सत्रह (satrah, 17), अठारह (athaarah, 18), उन्नीस (unnees, 19), बीस (bees, 20).

The final ह of 11 to 18 is weak; in speech these sound like 'gyaara', 'baara', 'tera' and so on.

उन्नीस (19) is literally 'one less than twenty'. The same idea, उन- (un-) before the next ten, gives 29, 39, 49 and so on up to 79: उनतीस (untees, 29), उनतालीस (untaalees, 39). The last two are different: 89 is नवासी (navaasee) and 99 is निन्यानवे (ninyaanve).

guide.title: The tens, and the numbers in between
guide.text:
The tens are: दस (das, 10), बीस (bees, 20), तीस (tees, 30), चालीस (chaalees, 40), पचास (pachaas, 50), साठ (saath, 60), सत्तर (sattar, 70), अस्सी (assee, 80), नब्बे (nabbe, 90), सौ (sau, 100).

The numbers in between are a real challenge: Hindi has a separate fused word for every number up to 100. The unit comes first and the ten second, both worn down: इक्कीस (ikkees, 21) is 'one-twenty', पच्चीस (pachchees, 25) is 'five-twenty', पैंतालीस (paintaalees, 45) is 'five-forty', पचहत्तर (pachhattar, 75) is 'five-seventy', निन्यानवे (ninyaanve, 99) is 'nine-ninety'.

Do not try to learn all hundred at once. Learn the tens, 25, 50 and 75 first; you can understand most prices with those. And you can always fall back on English numbers, which every shopkeeper knows.

Above a hundred it becomes regular: एक सौ बीस (120), दो सौ (200), हज़ार (hazaar, 1,000). Large sums are counted in लाख (laakh, 100,000) and करोड़ (karor, 10 million), not in millions.

guide.title: Halves and quarters
guide.text:
Hindi has special words for fractions, used all the time with money, weights and clock times.

आधा (aadhaa): half. आधा किलो, 'half a kilo'.
डेढ़ (derh): one and a half. डेढ़ सौ is 150, डेढ़ किलो is a kilo and a half.
ढाई (dhaaee): two and a half. ढाई सौ is 250.
साढ़े (saarhe): plus a half, used from three upwards. साढ़े तीन सौ is 350.
सवा (savaa): plus a quarter. सवा सौ is 125.
पौने (paune): minus a quarter. पौने दो सौ is 175.

examples.english: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.

guide.title: Bargaining and paying
guide.text:
In markets and small shops without price tags, bargaining is expected and good-humoured. The classic moves are यह बहुत महँगा है ('this is very expensive') and थोड़ा कम कीजिए ('make it a little less'), followed by your own offer with में. In shops with fixed prices ('fixed price' is the phrase used) it is not done.

मिलना (milnaa), 'to be available, to be got', is the shop verb: इससे बड़ा साइज़ मिलेगा? 'Will a bigger size be available?' And चलना (chalnaa, 'to go, to work') asks whether something is accepted: क्या कार्ड चलेगा? 'Will a card do?'

examples.english: Please reduce the price a little.
Give it to me for a hundred rupees.

phrases.english: Please reduce the price a little.
phrases.note: The standard bargaining phrase.

phrases.english: Give it to me for a hundred rupees.
Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.

phrases.note: 'mujhe ... chaahiye' = 'I want / need ...'.

phrases.english: Do you have a bigger size?

phrases.note: A woman says: मैं बस देख रही हूँ (... dekh rahee hoon).

units.title: Family
units.description: Introduce your family, say how many brothers, sisters and children you have, and ask about someone else's.

guide.title: A precise word for every relative
guide.text:
Hindi kinship words are much more exact than English ones. They tell you the side of the family and often the relative age.

Parents: माँ (maan) or माता जी (maataa jee), mother; पिता जी (pitaa jee), father. At home most people say मम्मी and पापा. माता-पिता (maataa-pitaa) is 'parents'.

Grandparents: दादा and दादी (daadaa, daadee) are your father's parents; नाना and नानी (naanaa, naanee) are your mother's.

Uncles and aunts: चाचा (chaachaa) is your father's younger brother and चाची his wife; मामा (maamaa) is your mother's brother and मामी his wife; बुआ (buaa) is your father's sister; मौसी (mausee) is your mother's sister.

Brothers and sisters: भाई (bhaaee), brother; बहन (bahan, said 'behen'), sister. बड़ा (big) and छोटा (small) mean elder and younger: बड़ा भाई, छोटी बहन. An elder brother is addressed as भैया (bhaiyaa) and an elder sister as दीदी (deedee), not by name.

Children and spouses: बेटा (betaa), son; बेटी (betee), daughter; बच्चे (bachche), children; पति (pati), husband; पत्नी (patnee), wife.

examples.native: मेरे दादाजी गाँव में रहते हैं।
examples.roman: mere daadaajee gaanv mein rahte hain.
examples.english: My grandfather lives in the village.

guide.title: Respect inside the family
guide.text:
Older relatives are always spoken of in the respectful plural. That is why 'this is my mother' is ये मेरी माँ हैं, with ये and हैं, and 'my grandfather lives' is मेरे दादाजी रहते हैं, with मेरे and the plural verb, although there is only one grandfather.

The ending जी (jee) is attached to the words for older relatives: पिताजी, माताजी, दादाजी, चाचाजी. It may be written joined or separately.

A husband or wife is also introduced in the plural: ये मेरी पत्नी हैं, ये मेरे पति हैं. Children and younger brothers and sisters take the ordinary singular: यह मेरा बेटा है, 'this is my son'.

guide.title: How many do you have?
guide.text:
As you learnt in the unit on 'have', relatives are possessed with the plain possessive and 'to be': मेरे दो बच्चे हैं, 'my two children are', means 'I have two children'.

The plurals you need here: भाई does not change (दो भाई). बहन adds -en: दो बहनें (do bahnen). बेटा becomes बेटे; बेटी becomes बेटियाँ (betiyaan); बच्चा becomes बच्चे.

To ask: आपके कितने भाई-बहन हैं? 'How many brothers and sisters do you have?' आपके परिवार में कितने लोग हैं? 'How many people are there in your family?' Questions about family, marriage and children are ordinary friendly conversation in India, even between people who have just met.

examples.english: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

guide.title: Married?
guide.text:
शादी (shaadee) is 'wedding, marriage'. 'Are you married?' is asked as क्या आपकी शादी हो गई है?, literally 'has your marriage happened?'. The adjective शादीशुदा (shaadeeshudaa) means 'married' and does not change for gender: मैं शादीशुदा हूँ.

To say you are not married: मेरी शादी नहीं हुई है, 'my marriage has not happened'.

examples.native: क्या आपकी शादी हो गई है?
examples.roman: kyaa aapkee shaadee ho gaee hai?

phrases.note: Plural ये and हैं for respect.
The ending -jee shows respect.
Younger brother: छोटा भाई (chhotaa bhaaee).
बहन is pronounced 'behen'.

phrases.english: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

phrases.native: क्या आपकी शादी हो गई है?
phrases.roman: kyaa aapkee shaadee ho gaee hai?

phrases.note: The same for men and women.
For 'husband': ये मेरे पति हैं (ye mere pati hain).

phrases.native: मेरी बेटी स्कूल में पढ़ती है।
phrases.roman: meree betee skool mein parhtee hai.
phrases.literal: my daughter school in studying is

phrases.native: आपके परिवार में कितने लोग हैं?
phrases.roman: aapke parivaar mein kitne log hain?
phrases.english: How many people are there in your family?
phrases.literal: your family in how-many people are

phrases.native: मेरे माता-पिता भारत में रहते हैं।
phrases.roman: mere maataa-pitaa bhaarat mein rahte hain.
phrases.literal: my mother-father India in living are

phrases.native: मेरे दादाजी गाँव में रहते हैं।
phrases.roman: mere daadaajee gaanv mein rahte hain.
phrases.english: My grandfather lives in the village.
phrases.literal: my grandfather village in living are
phrases.note: दादाजी is your father's father; your mother's father is नानाजी (naanaajee).

units.title: Time, days and dates
units.description: Ask and tell the time, name the days, and talk about today, tomorrow and yesterday.

guide.title: Telling the time
guide.text:
The clock uses the verb बजना (bajnaa), 'to strike, to ring'. 'What time is it?' is कितने बजे हैं?, literally 'how many have struck?'. The answer is the number plus बजे हैं: पाँच बजे हैं, 'it is five o'clock'. One o'clock is singular: एक बजा है.

The fraction words from the shopping unit do the work of 'half past' and 'quarter': साढ़े तीन बजे (half past three), सवा तीन बजे (quarter past three), पौने चार बजे (quarter to four). Two special cases: half past one is डेढ़ बजे (derh baje) and half past two is ढाई बजे (dhaaee baje).

'At' a time needs no postposition; बजे by itself means 'at ... o'clock': हम सात बजे मिलेंगे, 'we will meet at seven'. 'At what time?' is कितने बजे?

For minutes, people say दस बजकर बीस मिनट ('twenty past ten', literally 'having struck ten, twenty minutes'), or just read the digits: दस बीस.

examples.english: We will meet at seven o'clock.

guide.title: Yesterday and tomorrow are the same word
guide.text:
आज (aaj) is 'today'. कल (kal) means both 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow', one day away from today in either direction, and the tense of the verb tells you which: मैं कल आऊँगा, 'I will come tomorrow'; मैं कल आया था, 'I came yesterday'. In the same way परसों (parson) is both 'the day after tomorrow' and 'the day before yesterday'.

अभी (abhee) is 'right now'; अब (ab) is 'now'; बाद में (baad mein) is 'later'; पहले (pahle) is 'earlier, before'.

Parts of the day: सुबह (subah, morning), दोपहर (dopahar, midday, afternoon), शाम (shaam, evening), रात (raat, night). 'In the evening' and 'at night' take को: शाम को, रात को. सुबह is usually used without it. Combine them freely: कल सुबह ('tomorrow morning' or 'yesterday morning'), आज रात ('tonight').

examples.english: The day after tomorrow is a holiday.

guide.title: Days of the week
guide.text:
The days all end in -वार (-vaar, 'day'): सोमवार (somvaar, Monday), मंगलवार (mangalvaar, Tuesday), बुधवार (budhvaar, Wednesday), गुरुवार (guruvaar, Thursday), शुक्रवार (shukravaar, Friday), शनिवार (shanivaar, Saturday), रविवार (ravivaar, Sunday).

Thursday is also called बृहस्पतिवार (brihaspativaar), and Sunday is very often इतवार (itvaar).

'On Monday' is सोमवार को. हफ़्ता (haftaa) is 'week', महीना (maheenaa) 'month', साल (saal) 'year'. 'Next' is अगला and 'last' is पिछला; with को understood they take the oblique: अगले हफ़्ते ('next week'), पिछले साल ('last year'), अगले महीने ('next month').

examples.english: I will come on Saturday. (man speaking)
I will go to India next month. (man speaking)

guide.title: Dates and months
guide.text:
The months used in daily life are the international ones with a Hindi accent: जनवरी (janvaree), फ़रवरी (farvaree), मार्च (maarch), अप्रैल (aprail), मई (maee), जून (joon), जुलाई (julaaee), अगस्त (agast), सितंबर (sitambar), अक्टूबर (aktoobar), नवंबर (navambar), दिसंबर (disambar).

तारीख (taareekh) is 'date'. Dates are given as number, तारीख, and को for 'on': पाँच तारीख को, 'on the fifth'; दस मार्च को, 'on the tenth of March'.

Useful words about time: समय (samay) and वक्त (vakt) both mean 'time'; देर (der) is 'lateness, delay'; जल्दी (jaldee) is 'early, soon, quickly'.

phrases.note: Singular बजा है, because it is only one.

phrases.english: We will meet at seven o'clock.

phrases.note: 'kal' means both tomorrow and yesterday; the verb tense tells which. A woman says आऊँगी (aaoongee).
A woman says: मैं कल आई थी (main kal aaee thee).

phrases.english: The day after tomorrow is a holiday.
phrases.note: परसों can also mean 'the day before yesterday'.

phrases.english: I will go to India next month.
phrases.note: A woman says: ... जाऊँगी (jaaoongee).

phrases.native: अभी मेरे पास समय नहीं है।
phrases.roman: abhee mere paas samay naheen hai.
phrases.english: I don't have time right now.
phrases.literal: right-now my near time not is
phrases.note: 'mere paas' (near me) is how Hindi says 'I have'.

units.title: Weather and seasons
units.description: Talk about heat, cold, rain and the seasons, and say how the weather feels to you.

guide.title: Weather is a noun
guide.text:
English says 'it is hot'. Hindi has no 'it'; it says that heat exists: गर्मी है (garmee hai), 'there is heat'. Likewise ठंड है (thand hai), 'there is cold', 'it is cold'.

Keep the nouns and the adjectives apart. गर्मी (garmee) is the noun 'heat' and also 'summer'; गर्म (garm) is the adjective 'hot'. ठंड (thand) and सर्दी (sardee) are the nouns 'cold'; ठंडा (thandaa) is the adjective. For the weather use the nouns: आज बहुत गर्मी है. For things use the adjectives: चाय गर्म है, पानी ठंडा है.

मौसम (mausam) means both 'weather' and 'season': आज मौसम कैसा है? 'How is the weather today?'

guide.title: Rain falls, wind moves, sun is strong
guide.text:
Each kind of weather has its own verb, and the verb agrees with the weather noun.

बारिश (baarish, rain, feminine) 'happens': बारिश हो रही है, 'it is raining'; कल बारिश होगी, 'it will rain tomorrow'.
हवा (havaa, wind, air, feminine) 'moves': हवा चल रही है, 'the wind is blowing'.
धूप (dhoop, sunshine, feminine) 'is strong' or 'has come out': धूप बहुत तेज़ है; धूप निकली है, 'the sun is out'.
बादल (baadal, clouds, masculine) 'have spread': बादल छाए हैं, 'it is cloudy'.
बर्फ़ (barf, snow, ice, feminine) 'falls': बर्फ़ गिर रही है, 'it is snowing'.

guide.title: How it feels to you
guide.text:
To say that you feel hot or cold, the heat or cold 'attaches' to you, with the same verb लगना you met with hunger: मुझे ठंड लग रही है, 'I am feeling cold'; मुझे गर्मी लग रही है, 'I am feeling hot'.

Do not say मैं ठंडा हूँ or मैं गर्म हूँ for this. Applied to a person these adjectives describe temperament or worse, not body temperature.

Likes and dislikes use पसंद (pasand) with the same 'to me' pattern: मुझे सर्दी पसंद है, 'I like winter'.

guide.title: The seasons
guide.text:
North India speaks of three main seasons: गर्मी (garmee), the hot season from about April to June; बरसात (barsaat) or मानसून (maansoon), the rains from about July to September; and सर्दी (sardee), the cool season from about November to February. वसंत (vasant) is spring.

'In summer' and 'in winter' are commonly said in the plural: गर्मियों में (garmiyon mein), सर्दियों में (sardiyon mein). With गर्मी, ठंड and बारिश the verb पड़ना ('to fall') describes how severe it gets: यहाँ बहुत गर्मी पड़ती है, 'it gets very hot here'.

units.title: Health and emergencies
units.description: Get help, describe what is wrong with you and report something lost or stolen.

guide.title: Calling for help
guide.text:
The shout for help is बचाओ! (bachaao!), literally 'save (me)!'. To ask someone calmly for help, say मेरी मदद कीजिए, 'please do my help'. मदद (madad) is feminine, hence मेरी.

To have someone fetched, use बुलाइए (bulaaiye, 'please call, please summon') with को after the person: डॉक्टर को बुलाइए, पुलिस को बुलाइए. With a thing rather than a person, को is not needed: एंबुलेंस बुलाइए.

In India the single emergency number is 112. पुलिस (pulis), एंबुलेंस (embulens) and अस्पताल (aspataal, hospital) are understood everywhere.

guide.title: Saying what is wrong
guide.text:
Illnesses are 'to' you: मुझे बुखार है (bukhaar, fever), मुझे खाँसी है (khaansee, a cough), मुझे ज़ुकाम है (zukaam, a cold), मुझे दस्त हैं (dast, diarrhoea, plural).

The general statement is मेरी तबीयत ठीक नहीं है, 'my state of health is not right'. तबीयत (tabeeyat) is feminine.

Sensations 'come': मुझे चक्कर आ रहा है, 'dizziness is coming to me', 'I feel dizzy'; मुझे उल्टी आ रही है, 'I feel sick'.

An injury 'strikes': मुझे चोट लगी है (chot, injury), 'I am hurt'.

guide.title: Where it hurts
guide.text:
दर्द (dard) is 'pain'. Name the part of the body, add में ('in'), then दर्द है: मेरे पेट में दर्द है, 'there is pain in my stomach'. Or simply point and say यहाँ दर्द हो रहा है, 'it is hurting here'.

Parts of the body: सिर (sir, head), पेट (pet, stomach), गला (galaa, throat), दाँत (daant, tooth), आँख (aankh, eye), कान (kaan, ear), हाथ (haath, hand, arm), पैर (pair, foot, leg), पीठ (peeth, back), सीना (seenaa, chest).

Remember the oblique: गला becomes गले में, सीना becomes सीने में. And मेरा becomes मेरे before a masculine noun with में: मेरे सिर में दर्द है.

दवा (davaa) is 'medicine'; a pharmacy is दवा की दुकान, 'medicine shop', also called 'medical store' or 'chemist'.

guide.title: Lost and stolen
guide.text:
'To get lost' is खो जाना (kho jaanaa) and 'to be stolen' is चोरी हो जाना (choree ho jaanaa). The verb agrees with the lost thing, not with you: मेरा फ़ोन खो गया है (फ़ोन is masculine), मेरी चाबी खो गई है (चाबी, key, is feminine), मेरे पैसे चोरी हो गए हैं (पैसे is plural).

Notice that Hindi says 'my phone has got lost', not 'I have lost my phone'. For the important document: मेरा पासपोर्ट खो गया है.

units.title: Phone and appointments
units.description: Make and answer a phone call, ask for someone, and fix a time to meet.

guide.title: Opening a call
guide.text:
Calls open with हेलो (helo). To ask who is calling, say कौन बोल रहे हैं?, 'who is speaking?', using the polite plural because you do not know the caller. To identify yourself, say your name and बोल रहा हूँ ('am speaking'): मैं राज बोल रहा हूँ, 'this is Raj speaking'. A woman says बोल रही हूँ.

To ask for someone, use से बात करना, 'to talk with': क्या मैं अमित से बात कर सकता हूँ? 'May I speak to Amit?' Add जी after the name for an older or senior person: अमित जी से.

If the person is out, you will hear something like वे अभी घर पर नहीं हैं ('he is not at home right now'), again with the respectful plural वे ... हैं.

guide.title: Calling, calling back, messages
guide.text:
'To phone' is फ़ोन करना (fon karnaa), and the person you call takes को: मैं आपको फ़ोन करूँगा, 'I will call you'. 'Later' is बाद में (baad mein). The present tense is often used for something you are about to do: मैं आपको पाँच मिनट में फ़ोन करता हूँ, 'I'll call you in five minutes'.

A message is मैसेज (maisej), and 'to send' is भेजना (bhejnaa): मैसेज भेज दीजिए.

When the line is bad: आवाज़ नहीं आ रही है, 'the sound is not coming', that is, 'I can't hear you'; ज़रा ज़ोर से बोलिए, 'please speak a bit louder'. ज़ोर से (zor se) is literally 'with force'.

Phone numbers are read out digit by digit, usually in English, though you will also hear Hindi digits. नंबर (nambar) is 'number', and a wrong number is गलत नंबर (galat nambar).

guide.title: Making an appointment
guide.text:
'To meet' or 'to see' someone is मिलना (milnaa), and the person you meet takes से: मुझे डॉक्टर से मिलना है, 'I need to see the doctor'.

For the appointment itself, people say समय (samay, 'time') or just the English 'appointment' (अपॉइंटमेंट). The time is linked with का: कल दस बजे का समय, 'a ten o'clock slot tomorrow'. मिलेगा? ('will it be available?') turns it into a request: कल दस बजे का समय मिलेगा?

To ask when someone is free: आप कब फ़्री हैं? The English 'free' is the everyday word; the Hindi खाली (khaalee) literally means 'empty'.

units.title: Travel and staying somewhere
units.description: Buy tickets, find your train and your seat, and deal with a hotel room.

guide.title: Rooms and what they cost
guide.text:
To ask for a room use मुझे ... चाहिए: मुझे एक कमरा चाहिए, 'I need a room'. To see it first, which is quite normal, say कमरा दिखाइए.

किराया (kiraayaa) is the rent or charge, and 'per night' is expressed with का: एक रात का कितना किराया है?, literally 'one night's how much rent is?'.

To ask whether the room has something, put कमरे में ('in the room') first: क्या कमरे में एसी है? Hotel vocabulary is largely English: एसी (esee, AC), वाई-फ़ाई (vaaee-faaee, Wi-Fi), चेकआउट (chekaaut, checkout). गर्म पानी is hot water, नाश्ता (naashtaa) is breakfast, and शामिल (shaamil) means 'included'.

guide.title: Tickets, trains and buses
guide.text:
A ticket 'to' a place is a ticket 'of' that place: दिल्ली का टिकट, 'a Delhi ticket'. (टिकट is treated as masculine by some speakers and feminine by others, so you will also hear दिल्ली की टिकट.)

For departure times ask कितने बजे? ('at what o'clock?'). The verb for a train or bus leaving is छूटना (chhootnaa) or निकलना (nikalnaa), and for arriving पहुँचना (pahunchnaa): ट्रेन कितने बजे छूटती है? 'What time does the train leave?'

Useful words: प्लेटफ़ॉर्म (pletform, platform), सीट (seet, seat), सामान (saamaan, luggage), खाली (khaalee, empty, free). To ask whether a seat is taken: यह सीट खाली है? ट्रेन (train) and बस (bus) are both feminine.

guide.title: The handy word vaalaa
guide.text:
वाला (vaalaa) turns almost any word into a description meaning 'the one with, the one of, the one for'. It agrees like an -aa adjective: वाला, वाली, वाले.

खिड़की वाली सीट is 'the window seat' ('the seat with the window'). दिल्ली वाली ट्रेन is 'the Delhi train'. ऊपर वाला कमरा is 'the upstairs room'. यह वाला is 'this one'.

After a noun it also names the person who deals in something: चाय वाला (the tea seller), ऑटो वाला (the auto-rickshaw driver), सब्ज़ी वाला (the vegetable seller).

After the -ने form of a verb it means 'about to': ट्रेन आने वाली है, 'the train is about to arrive'.

guide.title: Staying and stopping
guide.text:
रुकना (ruknaa) means both 'to stop' and 'to stay' somewhere temporarily: मैं तीन दिन रुकूँगा, 'I will stay three days'. For living somewhere permanently the verb is रहना (rahnaa). A period of time needs no word for 'for': तीन दिन, 'for three days'; एक हफ़्ता, 'for a week'.

When something in the room does not work, describe what is not happening: गर्म पानी नहीं आ रहा है, 'hot water is not coming'; एसी नहीं चल रहा है, 'the AC is not running'.

units.title: At work or study
units.description: Talk about your job or your studies, meetings, deadlines, exams and days off.

guide.title: Working, studying, teaching
guide.text:
काम (kaam) is 'work', and काम करना is 'to work': मैं एक कंपनी में काम करता हूँ, 'I work in a company'. The place of work takes में.

पढ़ना (parhnaa) means both 'to read' and 'to study': मैं कॉलेज में पढ़ता हूँ, 'I study at college'. Its partner पढ़ाना (parhaanaa) is 'to teach', literally 'to cause to read'. Many Hindi verbs come in such pairs, where an added -aa- means making someone else do the action: सीखना (to learn) and सिखाना (to teach a skill), समझना (to understand) and समझाना (to explain).

Job titles and workplaces are mostly English words: ऑफ़िस (ofis) alongside the Hindi दफ़्तर (daftar), कंपनी (kampnee), मैनेजर, मीटिंग (meeting), कॉलेज (kolej), स्कूल (skool).

guide.title: Noun + karnaa, noun + honaa
guide.text:
Hindi makes new verbs freely by putting करना ('to do') after a noun or adjective. With करना someone does the action; with होना ('to happen') instead, it happens by itself. Work life is full of these pairs.

शुरू करना (shuroo karnaa), to start something; शुरू होना, to start, to begin. मीटिंग दस बजे शुरू होगी, 'the meeting will start at ten'.
खत्म करना (khatm karnaa), to finish something; खत्म होना, to come to an end.
पूरा करना (pooraa karnaa), to complete; पूरा होना, to be completed.
बंद करना (band karnaa), to close, to switch off; बंद होना, to be closed.

English words slot into the same frame, which is how most modern office talk is built: ईमेल करना, फ़ोन करना, चेक करना ('to check'), कैंसल करना ('to cancel').

In the past tense the verbs made with करना follow the ne pattern, and the verb agrees with the object (those made with होना never take ने): मैंने काम पूरा कर लिया, 'I have finished the work'.

guide.title: Deadlines, exams and days off
guide.text:
तक (tak, 'until, by') gives a deadline: कल तक ('by tomorrow'), शुक्रवार तक ('by Friday'), कब तक? ('by when?'). यह काम कब तक करना है? is 'by when does this work have to be done?', using the 'have to' pattern of -ना है.

परीक्षा (pareekshaa) is 'examination'; students mostly say एग्ज़ाम. Like relatives and illnesses, an exam or a day off is not 'had' with के पास: you say कल मेरी परीक्षा है, 'tomorrow my exam is'.

छुट्टी (chhuttee) covers 'holiday', 'day off' and 'leave': आज मेरी छुट्टी है, 'today is my day off'. To ask for leave: मुझे कल छुट्टी चाहिए.

To ask permission to ask a question, drop the क्या and मैं as people do in speech: एक सवाल पूछ सकता हूँ? 'May I ask a question?'

units.title: Everyday conversation
units.description: Keep a simple conversation going: say when you don't understand, ask what words mean and make small talk.

guide.title: When you don't understand
guide.text:
Your most valuable phrases as a learner are the ones that slow the other person down.

मुझे समझ नहीं आया (mujhe samajh naheen aayaa), 'understanding did not come to me', is 'I didn't understand'. A fuller form you will also hear is मेरी समझ में नहीं आया, 'it did not come into my understanding'.

ज़रा धीरे बोलिए, 'please speak a little slowly'. धीरे (dheere) is 'slowly' and also 'quietly'.

एक बार फिर से कहिए, 'please say it once again'. एक बार is 'one time', फिर से is 'again'.

And when you are simply lost: मुझे नहीं पता (mujhe naheen pataa), 'I don't know'. पता (pataa) is 'knowledge of a fact' and takes the 'to me' pattern: आपको पता है? 'Do you know?'

guide.title: Asking about words
guide.text:
Turn every conversation into a lesson with two questions.

इसका क्या मतलब है? (iskaa kyaa matlab hai?), 'what is the meaning of this?'. मतलब (matlab) is 'meaning'; on its own, मतलब? is a quick 'meaning what?', and people also use it as a filler, like 'I mean'.

इसे क्या कहते हैं? (ise kyaa kahte hain?), literally 'what do (they) call this?'. Hindi uses 'they say' without a subject where English uses a passive. To ask for the Hindi word, begin with हिंदी में: हिंदी में इसे क्या कहते हैं?

Languages 'come' to you: क्या आपको अंग्रेज़ी आती है? 'Does English come to you?', that is, 'do you know English?'. You can equally ask with बोलना: क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?

examples.english: Do you speak Hindi? (to a man)

guide.title: Likes: the 'to me' pattern once more
guide.text:
By now you have met many sentences that start with मुझे rather than मैं: wanting, having to, illnesses, hunger, knowing a language. Liking belongs to the same family. मुझे यह जगह पसंद है, 'to me this place is pleasing', is 'I like this place'.

पसंद (pasand) never changes. Add बहुत for 'very much': मुझे यह बहुत पसंद है. The negative is पसंद नहीं है.

Whenever a Hindi sentence is about something you experience rather than something you actively do, expect मुझे, and expect the verb to agree with the thing experienced, not with you.

examples.native: मुझे यह जगह बहुत पसंद है।
examples.roman: mujhe yah jagah bahut pasand hai.

guide.title: Small talk and reactions
guide.text:
The weather is as safe a topic in Hindi as in English: आज बहुत गर्मी है, 'it is very hot today'.

React while the other person talks: अच्छा ('I see'), हाँ हाँ ('yes, yes'), सच में? (sach mein?, 'really?'), वाह! (vaah!, 'wow, bravo'), अरे! (are!, a cry of surprise). To show that you have understood: समझ गया, or from a woman समझ गई.

The all-purpose soother is कोई बात नहीं, 'no problem, never mind'.

To round off a pleasant chat: आपसे बात करके अच्छा लगा, 'it felt good talking with you'.

examples.english: It was nice talking to you.

phrases.note: Also used where English says 'I don't understand'.
'zaraa' (a little) softens the request; 'kripayaa' is a formal 'please'.
Literally 'Does English come to you?'
To a woman: ... बोलती हैं? (boltee hain?)
A woman says: ... बोलती हूँ (boltee hoon).
A woman says: अच्छा, समझ गई (achchhaa, samajh gaee).
Also the usual reply to 'sorry' or 'thank you'.

units.title: Feelings and opinions
units.description: Say how you feel, what you like and dislike, what you think, and whether you agree.

guide.title: Two ways to have a feeling
guide.text:
Some feelings are adjectives used with 'I am', as in English: मैं खुश हूँ (khush, happy), मैं परेशान हूँ (pareshaan, worried, bothered), मैं उदास हूँ (udaas, sad), मैं थका हुआ हूँ (tired). Adjectives such as खुश, परेशान and उदास do not change for gender.

Many others are nouns that come to you, strike you or happen to you, in the 'to me' pattern:

डर लगना (dar lagnaa): fear strikes. मुझे डर लग रहा है, 'I am scared'.
गुस्सा आना (gussaa aanaa): anger comes. मुझे गुस्सा आ रहा है, 'I am getting angry'.
दुख होना (dukh honaa): sorrow happens. मुझे दुख हुआ, 'I was saddened'.
खुशी होना (khushee honaa): happiness happens. मुझे बहुत खुशी हुई, 'I was very glad'.
याद आना (yaad aanaa): memory comes. मुझे आपकी याद आती है, 'I miss you', literally 'your memory comes to me'.

In these sentences the verb agrees with the feeling: डर and गुस्सा are masculine (लग रहा है, आ रहा है); खुशी and याद are feminine (हुई, आती है).

guide.title: Liking: three shades
guide.text:
पसंद है (pasand hai) states a standing preference: मुझे संगीत बहुत पसंद है, 'I like music very much'.

पसंद आया (pasand aayaa), 'came to be liked', is your reaction to something you have just tried: मुझे खाना पसंद आया, 'I liked the food'.

अच्छा लगना (achchhaa lagnaa), 'to feel good, to seem good', is the warmest and commonest: मुझे बहुत अच्छा लगा, 'I liked it a lot', 'that felt really nice'. Here अच्छा agrees with the thing liked: यह फ़िल्म मुझे अच्छी लगी.

To ask someone's reaction: आपको कैसा लगा? 'How did you like it?' To ask how they are feeling right now: आपको कैसा लग रहा है?

guide.title: Giving an opinion
guide.text:
'I think' is usually मुझे लगता है (mujhe lagtaa hai), 'it seems to me', followed by what you think. The linking word कि (ki, 'that') may be included or left out: मुझे लगता है (कि) आप सही हैं, 'I think you are right'.

Other openers: मेरे विचार से (mere vichaar se), 'in my opinion', and शायद (shaayad), 'perhaps'.

सही (sahee) is 'right, correct' and गलत (galat) is 'wrong'. To agree: मैं आपसे सहमत हूँ (sahmat), 'I agree with you', or more simply आप ठीक कह रहे हैं, 'you are right in what you say', or just हाँ, बिलकुल. To disagree gently: मुझे ऐसा नहीं लगता, 'I don't think so', literally 'it does not seem so to me'.

Describing things: मज़ेदार (mazedaar) is 'fun, enjoyable, tasty', बढ़िया (barhiyaa) is 'great', बेकार (bekaar) is 'useless, rubbish'.

examples.roman: mujhe lagtaa hai aap sahee hain.

guide.title: Reassuring someone
guide.text:
चिंता (chintaa) is 'worry'. चिंता मत कीजिए is 'don't worry', and चिंता की कोई बात नहीं is 'there is nothing to worry about', literally 'there is no matter of worry'. The pattern X की कोई बात नहीं is productive: डर की कोई बात नहीं, 'there is nothing to be afraid of'.

सब ठीक हो जाएगा, 'everything will be fine', is what you say next.

examples.english: There is nothing to worry about.
There is nothing to be afraid of.

phrases.note: The same for men and women: परेशान does not change, and थोड़ा is an adverb here. Many women also say मैं थोड़ी परेशान हूँ (main thoree pareshaan hoon).
Said on hearing bad news, like 'I am sorry to hear that'.

phrases.roman: mujhe lagtaa hai aap sahee hain.
phrases.literal: to-me seems is you right are

units.title: Joining sentences
units.description: Link ideas with and, or, but, because, so, that, if and when.

guide.title: And, or, but, also
guide.text:
और (aur) is 'and'. Remember that it is also 'more': और चाय?, 'more tea?'.

या (yaa) is 'or': चाय या कॉफ़ी?

'But' has three everyday words that mean the same: लेकिन (lekin), पर (par) and मगर (magar). लेकिन is the safest; पर is the shortest and very common in speech (do not confuse it with the postposition पर, 'on').

भी (bhee) is 'also, too'. Its position matters: it comes immediately after the word it applies to. मैं भी चलूँगा is 'I too will come (as well as the others)'; मैं खाना भी लाऊँगा is 'I will bring food too (as well as other things)'.

फिर भी (phir bhee) is 'even so, still': मैं थका हूँ, फिर भी काम करूँगा.

guide.title: Because, so, that
guide.text:
क्योंकि (kyonki) is 'because'. It introduces the reason, which follows the main statement: मैं नहीं आया क्योंकि मैं बीमार था, 'I didn't come because I was ill'.

इसलिए (isliye) is 'so, therefore', literally 'for this'. It introduces the result: बारिश हो रही थी, इसलिए मैं नहीं गया.

कि (ki) is 'that', linking a verb of saying, thinking or knowing to what is said, thought or known: उसने कहा कि ..., 'he said that ...'; मुझे पता है कि ..., 'I know that ...'. It is spelt with a short i; do not confuse it with की (kee, 's).

After कि Hindi keeps the words of the original thought, including its tense. 'He said that he would come tomorrow' is उसने कहा कि वह कल आएगा, literally 'he said that he will come tomorrow'. A question tucked inside a sentence also keeps its own shape: मुझे पता है कि वह कहाँ है, 'I know where he is'.

guide.title: If ... then, when ... then
guide.text:
Hindi likes its linking words in pairs: one opens the first half of the sentence and a partner opens the second.

अगर ... तो (agar ... to): if ... then. The तो is nearly always there, even though English usually drops 'then'. अगर बारिश हुई तो हम नहीं जाएँगे, 'if it rains, we won't go'. Notice the past form हुई in the 'if' half: Hindi often uses the past for a condition that may come true. The future is also correct: अगर बारिश होगी तो ....

जब ... तब (jab ... tab): when ... then. जब आप आएँगे, तब हम खाएँगे, 'when you come, we will eat'. Hindi uses the future in both halves, where English uses the present after 'when'. In speech तब is often replaced by तो.

Note that जब is the 'when' of statements. The 'when' of questions is कब: आप कब आएँगे?

नहीं तो (naheen to) is 'otherwise', literally 'if not, then'.

guide.title: The one who ...; first ... then
guide.text:
Words like 'who', 'which' and 'that' inside a sentence ('the man who is standing there') are जो (jo) in Hindi, and again there is a partner: the जो part usually comes first, and the main part picks it up with वह. जो वहाँ खड़ा है, वह मेरा भाई है, word for word 'who there standing is, he my brother is'.

To put actions in order use पहले (pahle, 'first'), फिर (phir, 'then') and उसके बाद (uske baad, 'after that'): पहले खाना खाइए, फिर दवा लीजिए.

There is also a compact way to say 'having done one thing, do another': add -कर (-kar) to the stem of the first verb. खाना खाकर आइए, 'come after eating'; आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई, 'having met you, I am glad'. With करना the form is करके (karke).

units.title: Dialogue: meeting someone on a train
units.description: Follow and take part in a complete first conversation with a stranger, line by line.

guide.title: The situation
guide.text:
Tom, a visitor from England, gets on a train to Jaipur and finds a free seat next to Anita, who is travelling home. The phrases of this unit are the lines of their conversation in order. The note on each line says who is speaking.

Read the whole dialogue through first, then practise each line. Nearly everything in it comes from earlier units: greetings, 'where are you from', the continuous tense, the future, and the 'to me' pattern.

The two speakers use आप to each other throughout, as strangers do. Because Tom is a man and Anita a woman, the dialogue also shows you both sets of verb endings side by side.

examples.native: नमस्ते, क्या यह सीट खाली है?
examples.roman: namaste, kyaa yah seet khaalee hai?

guide.title: Who is speaking to whom
guide.text:
Watch the verb endings change with the person being described.

Tom asks Anita आप कहाँ जा रही हैं?, with रही, because आप here is a woman. Anita answers मैं जयपुर जा रही हूँ, with रही for herself. When Tom speaks about himself he says जा रहा हूँ and सीख रहा हूँ.

When Anita asks Tom where he will stay, she says आप कहाँ रुकेंगे?, with the masculine ending -गे. To a woman it would be रुकेंगी. Her offer चाय पिएँगे? ('will you drink tea?') is masculine for the same reason.

If you are a woman, practise Tom's lines with रही, and expect questions put to you to end in रुकेंगी and पिएँगी. If you are a man, practise Anita's lines with रहा.

guide.title: Phrases worth stealing
guide.text:
आपकी हिंदी बहुत अच्छी है! You will hear this compliment after your first three words of Hindi. Languages are feminine, so आपकी and अच्छी. A modest reply is मैं अभी सीख रहा हूँ, 'I am still learning'; अभी, 'right now', gives the sense of 'still'.

भारत आपको कैसा लग रहा है?, 'how is India seeming to you?', is the question every visitor is asked. Answer with बहुत अच्छा. Replace भारत with any place or thing: दिल्ली आपको कैसी लग रही है? (दिल्ली is feminine).

यहाँ के लोग, 'the people of here', shows that के can follow यहाँ and वहाँ: यहाँ का खाना, 'the food here'.

आपसे मिलकर अच्छा लगा, 'it felt good to meet you', is a slightly warmer alternative to आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई.

units.title: Dialogue: at the market and in an auto
units.description: Follow and take part in two short real-life exchanges: buying fruit and taking an auto-rickshaw.

guide.title: The situation
guide.text:
Sara is buying mangoes from a fruit seller and then takes an auto-rickshaw to the station. The phrases of this unit are the lines of the two exchanges in order; the note on each line says who is speaking.

The first ten lines are the fruit stall, the last six the auto. Everything is built from the shopping, numbers and directions units, plus a few fixed expressions of the market that are explained below.

Sara calls the seller भैया (bhaiyaa, 'brother'), the normal friendly way to address a shopkeeper or driver. He calls her मैडम (maidam); a man would be called सर or भाई साहब.

examples.english: brother (to a shopkeeper, waiter or driver)

guide.title: The language of the market
guide.text:
आम कैसे दिए?, literally 'how (have you) given the mangoes?', is the market way of asking the price of something sold by weight. You can always use the textbook question instead: आम कितने के हैं?

Prices come without a verb: अस्सी रुपये किलो, 'eighty rupees a kilo'.

साठ में दीजिए, 'give (them) for sixty': में marks the price you are offering. The seller's सत्तर लगेंगे, 'seventy will be needed', uses लगना ('to cost, to take') in the future plural, agreeing with the unspoken रुपये.

Notice बहुत महँगे हैं with the plural ending -e, because the mangoes are plural.

दे दीजिए is the helper-verb version of दीजिए: 'do give me'.

कितने पैसे हुए?, 'how much money has it come to?', asks for the total. हुए is the past of होना, plural to agree with पैसे.

ये रहे आपके तीस रुपये, 'here are your thirty rupees': ये रहे (plural) and यह रहा or यह रही (singular) are what you say when handing something over or pointing it out.

examples.english: How much does it come to?

guide.title: Taking an auto
guide.text:
You hail an auto-rickshaw by calling ऑटो! and then ask whether the driver will go where you want: स्टेशन चलेंगे?, 'will you go to the station?'. चलना is used rather than जाना because you will be going along together.

कितना लेंगे?, 'how much will you take?', asks the fare. The driver's answer uses लगेंगे again: डेढ़ सौ रुपये लगेंगे, 'it will be a hundred and fifty rupees'.

If that seems high, ask for the meter (मीटर से चलिए) or make a lower offer with में, exactly as at the fruit stall. Once it is settled: ठीक है, चलिए, 'all right, let's go'.

examples.english: Will you go to the station?
